course.title: Physics II: Waves, Electricity and Magnetism, and Heat
course.description: Waves and light, electric and magnetic fields, induction, and heat and the limits on engines, with calculations that connect each idea to something you can measure.
course.audience: A capable adult who has finished Discere's mechanics course (forces, energy, momentum) and is comfortable with algebra and powers. Sines appear in the light lessons; a short recap is built in.

paragraphs: Much of physics beyond the motion of solid objects is about things you cannot see move. A note from a guitar reaches you because the air presses and relaxes in a pattern that travels at 343 m/s, while each small parcel of air stays where it was, and light crosses 150 million kilometres of empty space from the Sun in about eight minutes with nothing to carry it except changing electric and magnetic fields. Heat is hidden in the same way, since it is energy passing from a hotter body to a colder one, and you see it only through what it does, warming water or melting ice.

Each of these is governed by a short equation that gives a number you can check against a measurement. The speed of a wave is its frequency times its wavelength, the force between two charges falls with the square of the distance between them, and no engine working between 600 K and 300 K can turn more than half of its heat into work. With relations like these you can say where a lens will form an image, what voltage a transformer will deliver and how much heat leaks through a window, and you can see why every power station has to reject some of its heat to a river or the air, however well it is built.
outcomes: You'll be able to find the period and frequency of an oscillator and the speed, wavelength and frequency of a wave.
You'll be able to predict the harmonics of a string, the beat frequency of two notes, the fringes behind two slits and the shift in pitch from a moving source.
You'll be able to apply the decibel scale, Snell's law and the thin-lens equation to trace a ray and locate an image.
You'll be able to compute the force between charges, the field and voltage between plates, the force on a moving charge or a current, and the emf of a changing flux or a transformer.
You'll be able to calculate heat, conduction and radiation, and use the ideal gas law and the first law.
You'll be able to state the efficiency limit of an engine and explain why entropy rises.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Physics: Motion and Forces, Maths Foundations and Trigonometry, and assumes comfort with algebra, powers of ten and the sine of an angle.

modules.title: Oscillations, waves and light
modules.description: Things that repeat, how repeats travel as waves, and how light bends and forms images.

modules.title: Electricity and magnetism
modules.description: Charge, fields, voltage, magnetic force, induction and the electromagnetic wave.

modules.title: Heat and thermodynamics
modules.description: Temperature, heat, how energy moves, gases and the limit on engines.

concepts.title: Period and frequency
concepts.summary: The period T is the time for one cycle and the frequency f = 1/T is cycles per second (hertz).

concepts.title: Simple harmonic motion
concepts.summary: Motion under a restoring force proportional to displacement; a mass on a spring has T = 2 pi sqrt(m/k) and a small-angle pendulum has T = 2 pi sqrt(L/g).

concepts.title: Wave speed
concepts.summary: v = f x wavelength: speed equals frequency times the length of one cycle in space.

concepts.title: Transverse and longitudinal
concepts.summary: The medium moves across the direction of travel in transverse waves and along it in longitudinal waves; the wave carries energy, not matter.

concepts.title: Superposition
concepts.summary: Where waves overlap, their displacements add; peaks meeting peaks reinforce and peaks meeting troughs cancel.

concepts.title: Standing wave
concepts.summary: A string fixed at both ends supports waves with f_n = n v / (2L), where n = 1, 2, 3.

concepts.title: Decibel level
concepts.summary: Level = 10 log10(I / I0) with I0 = 1e-12 W/m2; every factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB.

concepts.title: Doppler shift
concepts.summary: For a source approaching a still listener, f' = f v / (v - v_source).

concepts.title: Refraction
concepts.summary: Light changes speed between media, v = c/n, and bends so that n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2).

concepts.title: Total internal reflection
concepts.summary: From a denser to a less dense medium, beyond the critical angle theta_c = arcsin(n2/n1) all the light reflects.

concepts.title: Thin-lens equation
concepts.summary: 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i, with magnification m = -d_i / d_o.

concepts.title: Real and virtual images
concepts.summary: A real image forms where rays meet and can be caught on a screen; a virtual image is where rays appear to come from.

concepts.title: Electric charge
concepts.summary: A conserved property that comes in two signs; like charges repel and unlike attract.

concepts.title: Coulomb's law
concepts.summary: F = k q1 q2 / r^2 with k = 8.99e9 N m2/C2.

concepts.title: Electric field
concepts.summary: E = F / q: the force per unit charge; between parallel plates E = V / d.

concepts.title: Potential difference
concepts.summary: The energy per unit charge: a charge q moved through V gains qV of energy.

concepts.title: Force on a moving charge
concepts.summary: F = q v B sin(theta), perpendicular to both v and B, so it changes direction but not speed.

concepts.title: Force on a wire
concepts.summary: F = B I L sin(theta) for a straight wire of length L carrying current I.

concepts.title: Faraday's law
concepts.summary: The induced emf is the rate of change of flux times the number of turns: emf = N x (change in flux)/(change in time).

concepts.title: Transformer
concepts.summary: Voltage ratios follow turn ratios: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.

concepts.title: Electromagnetic wave
concepts.summary: Changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other and travel at c = 3.00e8 m/s in a vacuum.

concepts.title: Spectrum
concepts.summary: Radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma are the same wave at different frequencies; c = f x wavelength.

concepts.title: Specific heat
concepts.summary: Q = m c deltaT; water's c is 4,186 J/(kg K).

concepts.title: Latent heat
concepts.summary: Energy to change phase at a fixed temperature: fusion of ice 334 kJ/kg, vaporisation of water 2,260 kJ/kg.

concepts.title: Conduction
concepts.summary: Rate = k A deltaT / L through a layer of conductivity k, area A and thickness L.

concepts.title: Radiation
concepts.summary: A surface at temperature T (in kelvin) emits power epsilon sigma A T^4, with sigma = 5.67e-8 W/(m2 K4).

concepts.title: Ideal gas law
concepts.summary: PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J/(mol K) and T in kelvin.

concepts.title: First law
concepts.summary: The change in internal energy equals the heat added minus the work done by the gas: delta U = Q - W.

concepts.title: Carnot limit
concepts.summary: No engine between a hot reservoir at T_h and a cold one at T_c exceeds 1 - T_c/T_h (kelvin).

concepts.title: Entropy
concepts.summary: Heat Q entering at temperature T changes entropy by Q/T; the total never decreases in a real process.

lessons.title: Things that repeat

lead.text: In the figure the 0.5 kg mass has been pulled 4 cm above its resting position and released at time zero. It rises and falls along the same path again and again, and one complete trip, from the top down to the bottom and back up to the top, is called a **cycle**. The greatest distance the mass reaches from its resting position, 4 cm here, is the **amplitude**.

afterFigure.text: The time taken by one cycle is the **period**, written T, and in the figure it is the distance along the time axis between two successive peaks, 0.314 s. The number of cycles in each second is the **frequency**, written f, and since one cycle takes 0.314 s, a whole second holds 1 ÷ 0.314 = 3.18 cycles. That gives the relation *f = 1/T*, or equally T = 1/f, and the unit of frequency is the **hertz** (Hz), where 1 Hz means one cycle per second.
Period and frequency therefore carry the same information, but they are different numbers: **a long period means a low frequency**.

diagram.alt: A graph of displacement against time for a mass on a spring: a repeating wave of height 4 cm, with one cycle of 0.314 s marked between two peaks.
diagram.caption: Displacement of the 0.5 kg mass over 0.8 s. The amplitude is the height of a peak; the period is the time between peaks.

reveal.text: Four cycles fit into each second, so this pendulum has a frequency of 4 Hz. A short period always goes with a high frequency.
The period is unchanged, 0.314 s. The smaller stretch gives a weaker pull and a gentler acceleration, which exactly offsets the shorter distance, and the next screen shows why.

lead.text: A spring pulls the mass back towards its resting position with a force proportional to how far it has been moved, F = −kx, where x is the displacement and k, the **stiffness**, is the force per metre of stretch (200 N/m for this spring). A force that always points back towards the resting position is a **restoring force**, and motion under a restoring force proportional to displacement is called **simple harmonic motion**.

Doubling the displacement doubles the force and so doubles the acceleration, which is why a smaller swing is slower but also shorter, and why the two effects cancel exactly. **The period does not depend on the amplitude.**

afterFigure.text: Calculus turns F = −kx into the result *T = 2π√(m/k)*. A larger mass accelerates less for the same force, so it makes T longer, while a stiffer spring pulls harder, so it makes T shorter. Quadrupling the mass doubles the period, since the square root of 4 is 2, and quadrupling the stiffness halves it.
If the spring hangs vertically, gravity moves the resting position down by a fixed amount but leaves the period unchanged.

diagram.alt: Three graphs of displacement against time for a spring with the same 3 cm swing. Period 0.314 s for 0.5 kg and 200 N/m, 0.628 s for 2 kg and 200 N/m, and 0.157 s for 0.5 kg and 800 N/m.
diagram.caption: The same swing for three masses and springs. Use the buttons to compare the periods.

steps.headline: Find the period and frequency of a 0.5 kg mass on a spring with k = 200 N/m.

workedSteps.text: Write the formula for a mass on a spring.
Divide the mass by the stiffness. In kilograms and newtons per metre the unit of the result is seconds squared.
Take the square root.
Multiply by 2π to get the period.
The frequency is the reciprocal of the period.

steps.headline: Find the period of a 2.0 kg mass on a spring with k = 50 N/m.

workedSteps.text: Write the formula.
Divide the mass by the stiffness.
Take the square root.
The root is then multiplied by 2π to give the period.

reveal.text: The periods are equal. The heavy bob is pulled harder by gravity, but it also has ten times the mass to accelerate, and the two effects cancel.

lead.text: A bob of mass m on a string of length L, swung a short way aside, is pulled back towards the bottom by the part of its weight that acts along its path. For a small angle that part is very nearly mg × x/L, where x is the sideways distance, so the restoring force is once more proportional to displacement, with an effective stiffness of mg/L. Putting k = mg/L into the spring formula, the m on top and the m underneath cancel and leave *T = 2π√(L/g)*.

afterFigure.text: With L = 1 m and g = 9.8 m/s², T = 2π√(1/9.8) = 2.01 s, and in general **only the length and g set the period**. Because L sits under a square root, a pendulum four times as long takes 2 times as long to swing: the figure shows a 4 m pendulum with a period of 4.01 s. The formula holds for swings of a few degrees, since wide swings take slightly longer, which is why a clock pendulum moves through a small arc.

diagram.alt: A pendulum of length 1 m with period 2.01 s, and one of length 4 m with period 4.01 s, drawn at the same scale.
diagram.caption: Quadrupling the length doubles the period. The dashed bob is the 1 m pendulum.

reveal.text: The period grows as the square root of the length, so nine times the length gives three times the period. Tripling the period is a much smaller change than multiplying it by nine.

lead.text: At the end of its swing the bob stops for an instant, so all of its energy is stored in its height above the lowest point. As it swings down that stored energy becomes [[kinetic energy|The energy of motion, ½mv². Met in Physics: Motion and Forces.]], and at the lowest point the bob is moving fastest and has none of the height energy left.

afterFigure.text: A mass on a spring does the same with the energy stored in the spring: at the ends of its travel all of it is stretch energy ½kx², and as it passes the resting position all of it is ½mv². With friction ignored the total never changes, and for an amplitude A it equals ½kA²; the 0.5 kg mass pulled 4 cm holds ½ × 200 × 0.04² = 0.16 J. A larger amplitude holds more energy but does not change the period.

diagram.alt: Three pendulum positions with two bars each. At both ends of the swing the height energy bar is full and the motion energy bar is empty; at the lowest point it is the other way round.
diagram.caption: The same energy changes form twice in every cycle.

blocks.text: Hang a 0.5 kg mass from a spring with a stiffness of 200 newtons per metre, pull it down a few centimetres and let go, and it moves up and down about three times every second. A heavier mass on the same spring moves up and down more slowly, and a stiffer spring with the same mass moves faster. One equation gives the rate for the spring, and a close relative of the same equation gives it for the pendulum.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the period and frequency of a mass on a spring and of a pendulum, and say what changes them.
intro.whyItMatters: Waves, sound and light all start from something that repeats, so this lesson gives the vocabulary the rest of the course uses.

recap.keyIdea: The period is the time for one cycle and the frequency is its reciprocal; for a spring T = 2π√(m/k) and for a small-swing pendulum T = 2π√(L/g), with no dependence on amplitude.

blocks.text: You measured a repeating motion by its amplitude, its period T and its frequency f = 1/T, and found that a restoring force proportional to displacement gives a period fixed by the mass and stiffness whatever the size of the swing. A pendulum is the same motion with gravity as the restoring force, and its mass cancels, so only L and g remain.
Because both periods depend on a square root, changing a quantity by a factor of four changes the period by only a factor of two, which is the most useful rule for estimating answers.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson sends a repeating motion outward through a medium and asks how fast the resulting pattern travels.

lessons.title: A wave is a travelling pattern

reveal.text: The cork rises as each crest reaches it and falls after it has passed, and it stays close to where it started. The next screen shows the same thing for a bead on a rope.

lead.text: Shake one end of a long rope up and down and a crest runs along it. In the figure the crest, marked with a ring, moves 0.5 m to the right in each quarter of a second, but the orange bead fixed at 1.0 m does not travel at all: it rises to the top of its path, falls back, and sinks below the rope's resting line, always at the same place along the rope. The rope is the **medium** that carries the wave, and each of its parts oscillates about a fixed position.

afterFigure.text: A **wave** is therefore a pattern that moves through a medium, and the thing that travels is the *pattern and its energy*, not the material. The distance from one crest to the next, measured along the direction of travel, is the **wavelength**, written λ (the Greek letter lambda), and a wave on this rope has a wavelength of 2 m. The frequency f of the wave is the frequency with which each bead oscillates, which here is 1 Hz.

diagram.alt: Four snapshots of a wave on a rope at 0, 0.25, 0.5 and 0.75 seconds. A marked crest moves 0.5 m to the right each time while a bead fixed at 1.0 m only moves up and down.
diagram.caption: The crest travels along the rope but the bead stays at 1.0 m and moves only up and down. Use the buttons to step through time.

lead.text: The figure shows the same wave twice: as a snapshot of the whole rope at one instant, and as a record of the height of one point on it over time. In the first the crest-to-crest distance is the wavelength, 2 m; in the second the crest-to-crest time is the period, 1 s. One full wavelength of pattern passes any point in exactly one period, because every point repeats the motion of the one before it after that delay.

The pattern therefore advances by one wavelength in one period, and speed is distance divided by time, so *v = λ/T*. Since 1/T is the frequency, this is usually written **v = fλ**: the speed of the wave equals its frequency times its wavelength.

afterFigure.text: For the rope, 1 Hz × 2 m gives 2 m/s, which matches the crest moving 0.5 m in each 0.25 s of the earlier figure. The equation applies to every kind of wave, so any two of the three quantities give the third.

diagram.alt: Two graphs of the same rope wave. The first shows height against position with the wavelength of 2 m marked between crests. The second shows height against time at one point with the period of 1 s marked.
diagram.caption: The same wave seen two ways. Use the buttons to switch between the snapshot and the record at one point.

steps.headline: A note of 440 Hz travels through air at 343 m/s. Find its wavelength.

workedSteps.text: Write the wave equation and solve it for the wavelength.
workedSteps.math: v = fλ, so λ = v / f

workedSteps.text: Substitute the speed of sound in air at 20 °C and the frequency.
Divide. A hertz is one per second, so the seconds cancel and the answer is in metres.
A wavelength of 0.78 m is about the width of a doorway, which suits a note in the middle of the singing range.

reveal.text: The wavelength is 3 m, about the height of a ceiling. The prefix mega means a million, so 100 MHz is 1.00 × 10⁸ Hz.
The note travels at 343 m/s, the same speed as before. It is the wavelength that halves, from 0.78 m to 0.39 m, as the speed stays fixed and the frequency doubles.

lead.text: The speed of a wave depends on the properties of the medium it moves through: sound moves at about 343 m/s in air at 20 °C, at about 1480 m/s in water, and light moves at about 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. The frequency, on the other hand, is set by whatever shakes the medium, such as a string, a loudspeaker or a transmitter, and it does not change as the wave passes onwards. Since v = fλ, the wavelength is the quantity left to adjust.

A 440 Hz note passing from air into water keeps its 440 Hz, because the water at the boundary is shaken once for each shake of the air, and its speed rises from 343 to about 1480 m/s, so its wavelength grows from 0.78 m to 1480 / 440 = 3.36 m.

afterFigure.text: A fast medium gives a long wavelength, and a slow medium gives a short one.

lead.text: The rope wave is **transverse**: each bead moves at right angles to the direction in which the wave travels. A spring coil that is pushed and pulled along its own length carries another kind. A region of squeezed coils moves along the spring while each coil itself only moves back and forth along the line of travel. A wave of this kind is **longitudinal**.
In the figure the marked piece of the medium is orange in both cases; compare the direction of its motion with the arrow that gives the direction of the wave.

afterFigure.text: Sound in air is longitudinal: a loudspeaker cone pushes air molecules together in a compression, followed by a region where they are spread out, and the pattern travels while each molecule shuffles back and forth. Sound is not transverse, though a diagram of it is often drawn as a wavy line, which shows the pressure at each point and not the direction in which the air moves.

diagram.alt: Two waves compared. On a rope, a marked bead moves up and down across the direction the wave travels. In a spring coil, a marked coil moves back and forth along the direction the wave travels.
diagram.caption: The marked piece of the medium is shown in orange. Use the buttons to compare the two kinds of wave.

reveal.text: The particles move along the line of travel, since ultrasound is sound and every sound wave is longitudinal, while light and waves on a rope are transverse.
The frequency stays at 660 Hz, and the faster speed gives a longer wavelength.

lessons.orientation: Use v = fλ and tell transverse waves from longitudinal ones.
lessons.reviewLabel: A wave is a travelling pattern
lessons.nextAction: Add two waves together and see what makes standing waves and beats.

blocks.text: Sound crosses a room at 343 m/s, and light from a lamp crosses the same room at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, nearly a million times faster. Both are waves, as a ripple on a pond is, and in each case what travels outward from the source is a pattern, a run of crests or of squeezed and stretched air, that repeats at a steady rate as it goes.
A wave's speed is tied by one short relation to two other numbers: how often the pattern repeats at any one place, and how far apart its repeats are in space.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use v = fλ to find any one of speed, frequency and wavelength from the other two, and say whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal.
intro.whyItMatters: The rest of the course, from sound to light, uses this one relation.

recap.keyIdea: A wave is a travelling pattern with speed v = fλ, in which the medium moves across the direction of travel in a transverse wave and along it in a longitudinal wave.

blocks.text: The pattern moves while each bit of the medium only oscillates, and a pattern that repeats every period T with a length λ moves at v = λ/T = fλ. The medium fixes the speed and the source fixes the frequency, so when a wave crosses into a new medium its wavelength changes and its frequency does not.
Whether a wave is transverse or longitudinal depends on how the medium moves compared with the way the pattern travels, which puts sound in air in the second group.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson adds two waves together and finds that they can strengthen, cancel or trap each other into standing patterns.

lessons.title: When waves add

reveal.text: The rope is 5 cm high at that instant, and the pulses then carry on past each other unchanged, as if neither had been there. They do not bounce.

lead.text: Waves do not collide the way balls do. Where two waves pass through the same point, the displacement of the medium is the *sum* of the displacements each wave would have caused alone, which is called **superposition**.

When crest meets crest the displacements have the same sign and the sum is twice as high, a result called **constructive interference**. When one wave is shifted by half a cycle, so that crest meets trough, the displacements are equal and opposite and the sum is zero everywhere, which is **destructive interference**.

afterFigure.text: Once the waves have passed each other, each continues as it was, so the addition is only a description of the region where they overlap. Interference between two waves is therefore decided by *how far apart they are in their cycles*.

diagram.alt: Two sine waves drawn together with their sum below. When the waves are in step the sum has twice the height; when they are half a cycle apart the sum is a flat line.
diagram.caption: Add two equal waves point by point. Use the buttons to change how far apart the waves are.

reveal.text: The trough cancels part of the crest and leaves the rope 1.8 cm up. Only two waves of equal size, half a cycle apart, cancel completely.

lead.text: Pluck a guitar string and waves run along it in both directions, reflecting at the fixed ends, so that two waves moving in opposite directions are always present and always adding. For most frequencies the sum is a jumble. For a few it settles into a pattern that stays in place, called a **standing wave**, in which some points, the **nodes**, never move, and between them the string swings in loops whose middle points, the **antinodes**, move the most.

The two ends are fixed, so both must be nodes, and that allows only whole loops: a loop is half a wavelength, so L = n × λ/2 with n = 1, 2, 3, and so on. Putting λ = 2L/n into v = fλ gives *f = nv/(2L)*.

afterFigure.text: The lowest frequency, n = 1, is the **fundamental**, and the others, whose frequencies are 2, 3, 4 times larger, are its **harmonics**. For the 0.5 m string with a wave speed of 200 m/s the fundamental is 200 / (2 × 0.5) = 200 Hz, and the figure shows the first four modes at 200, 400, 600 and 800 Hz. **No other frequency fits.**

diagram.alt: A string 0.5 m long fixed at both ends, drawn vibrating in its first four modes. Orange dots mark the nodes, which never move. Mode n has n loops and a frequency of 200n hertz.
diagram.caption: The first four modes of a 0.5 m string with wave speed 200 m/s. Use the buttons to move between modes.

steps.headline: A string 0.75 m long carries waves at 330 m/s. Find its fundamental frequency and its third harmonic.

workedSteps.text: The frequencies of a string fixed at both ends are given by this formula, where n counts the loops.
For the fundamental, n = 1. Substitute the speed and the length.
The third harmonic has three loops and is three times the fundamental.
The figure's n = 3 mode shows the same shape: three loops, with two nodes between the ends.

steps.headline: A string 0.80 m long carries waves at 200 m/s. Find its fifth harmonic.

workedSteps.text: Write the formula.
Find the fundamental first, with n = 1.
The fifth harmonic is five times the fundamental.

reveal.text: The sound swells and fades four times a second. The next screen shows that this rate is the difference of the two frequencies.

lead.text: Two sources of 8 Hz and 10 Hz start in step, and so add to twice the height. The faster wave gains on the slower one by one cycle every half second, so after a quarter of a second they are half a cycle apart and cancel, and after half a second they are in step again. The sum swells and fades twice each second, which is exactly the difference 10 − 8.

afterFigure.text: For sound the effect is heard as a wavering in loudness called **beats**, and the **beat frequency** is |f₁ − f₂|. There is no third wave: the beats are the sum of the two waves, whose pitch is close to their average and whose loudness follows the dashed envelope.

diagram.alt: Two waves of nearby frequencies added together: the sum swells and fades, with a dashed envelope. At 8 and 10 Hz it swells twice in one second; at 8 and 12 Hz, four times.
diagram.caption: The sum of two close frequencies, drawn with slow frequencies so the cycles can be counted. Use the buttons to change the gap.

lead.text: Around 1801 Thomas Young passed light through two narrow slits close together and saw on a screen beyond them a row of bright and dark bands, called **fringes**. Each slit acts as a source of waves that spread out behind it, and at a point on the screen the two waves have travelled different distances. Where the two distances differ by a whole number of wavelengths the waves arrive in step and the screen is bright, and where they differ by half a wavelength more they cancel and the screen is dark.
For a small angle the distance between neighbouring bright fringes is *y = λL/d*, where L is the distance to the screen and d is the separation of the slits.

afterFigure.text: A stream of tiny balls through two slits would make two bright patches, one behind each slit. Only waves that add give the row of fringes. With light of 500 nm, slits 0.10 mm apart and a screen 2.0 m away, y = 500 × 10⁻⁹ × 2.0 / 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.010 m = 1.0 cm, and doubling the separation to 0.20 mm halves the spacing to 0.5 cm, as the second button shows.

diagram.alt: A light beam passes two slits and reaches a screen 2.0 m away, where it forms a row of bright fringes. With slits 0.10 mm apart the fringes are 1.0 cm apart; with slits 0.20 mm apart they are 0.5 cm apart.
diagram.caption: Bright fringes on the screen for light of 500 nm. Doubling the slit separation halves the fringe spacing. Distances along the beam are not to scale.

lessons.orientation: Predict standing waves, beats and double-slit fringes from superposition.
lessons.nextAction: Bring in sound level and the Doppler shift, which depend on how loud a wave is and how its source moves.

blocks.text: Pluck a guitar string 0.5 m long and it sounds a note of 200 Hz, along with fainter notes at whole-number multiples of 200 Hz, while the frequencies in between are missing altogether. Strike two tuning forks a few hertz apart and the sound swells and fades in a slow, regular throb, and shine light through two narrow slits in a card and the screen beyond shows a row of bright and dark bands.
The three effects look unrelated, yet each of them follows from one rule about what happens where two waves pass through the same place.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the harmonics of a string, count beats from two frequencies and calculate the fringe spacing of a double slit.
intro.whyItMatters: Superposition explains musical pitch, tuning by ear and the fact that light behaves as a wave.

recap.keyIdea: Where waves overlap their displacements add, which gives standing waves with f = nv/(2L), beats at |f₁ − f₂| and fringes spaced by λL/d.

blocks.text: Two waves passing through the same region add their displacements and then continue unchanged, so crest meeting crest strengthens the wave and crest meeting trough cancels it. A string fixed at both ends supports only the frequencies f = nv/(2L), the beat frequency of two close pitches is their difference, and light through two slits forms fringes whose spacing is λL/d.
In each case the outcome depends only on how far apart the waves are in their cycles at the point where they meet.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to sound itself, to how loudness is measured in decibels and to how motion changes the pitch you hear.

lessons.title: Loudness, pitch and moving sources

lead.text: A scale in which every number is a multiple of the quietest sound would run from 1 to 1 000 000 000 000, so sound is described instead by a **level** in **decibels** (dB), defined as *L = 10 log₁₀(I / I₀)*, where I is the intensity and I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m² is the reference.

The [[logarithm|log₁₀ of a number is the power of 10 that gives it, so log₁₀ 1000 = 3.]] counts powers of ten, and that makes the figure a straight line: **every factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB**.

afterFigure.text: At the threshold of hearing I = I₀, the ratio is 1, log₁₀ 1 = 0, and the level is 0 dB. An intensity of 10⁻⁶ W/m² is a million times the reference, log₁₀ of a million is 6, and the level is 60 dB, about the level of ordinary conversation. At 1 W/m² the level is 120 dB.

diagram.alt: A graph with sound intensity on a logarithmic axis from 10 to the minus 12 to 1 watt per square metre, and sound level from 0 to 120 decibels. The graph is a straight line rising 10 decibels for every factor of 10 in intensity.
diagram.caption: Level against intensity. A trillion-fold range of intensity becomes a straight line from 0 to 120 dB.

steps.headline: A sound has an intensity of 1.0 × 10⁻³ W/m². Find its level in decibels.

workedSteps.text: Write the definition of the level.
Divide the intensity by the reference intensity, 10⁻¹² W/m².
The next move is the logarithm of that ratio.
Multiply by 10 to get decibels.

reveal.text: The level is 80 dB, 10 dB more. Ten times as many machines give ten times the intensity, and ten times the intensity adds just 10 dB.

lead.text: The rule *ΔL = 10 log₁₀(I₂/I₁)* gives the change in level when the intensity changes by the factor I₂/I₁. A factor of 10 gives +10 dB, a factor of 100 gives +20 dB, and a factor of 2 gives 10 log₁₀ 2 = 3.01 dB, about 3 dB. Two identical machines therefore sound 3 dB louder than one.

afterFigure.text: A level is not a quantity that doubles when the sound doubles. **A doubling of the intensity is a step of 3 dB**, and a rise of 10 dB, which is ten times the intensity, is heard as roughly twice as loud. A sound of 80 dB is therefore not twice as loud as one of 40 dB: it has ten thousand times the intensity.

diagram.alt: Four bars for the sound level of 1, 2, 10 and 100 identical machines: 70, 73, 80 and 90 decibels. The bars grow slowly although the number of machines grows a hundredfold.
diagram.caption: Each machine on its own gives 70 dB. Ten times as many machines adds only 10 dB.

reveal.text: The level rises by about 4.8 dB, to about 74.8 dB, since the intensity has tripled. That lies between the 3 dB of a doubling and the 10 dB of a factor of ten, as it must.
The pitch is higher than 500 Hz while it approaches and lower after it has passed, though the siren itself sounds at 500 Hz throughout. The next screen shows why.

lead.text: Each wave front leaves the source at the moment the source is at its centre, and then spreads out as a circle at the speed of sound, whatever the source does afterwards. A source that keeps moving therefore catches up with its own earlier fronts: ahead of it the circles are closer together than at rest, and behind it they are further apart. In one period the source covers the distance v_s T, so the wavelength ahead is shorter by that amount, λ' = (v − v_s)T.

The wave still moves at v, so the listener ahead receives f' = v/λ', which gives *f' = f v/(v − v_s)*. Behind the source the wavelength is longer by the same amount and f' = f v/(v + v_s). This change of the received frequency caused by motion is the **Doppler shift**.

afterFigure.text: The source itself still emits exactly f in every case, and so a siren is not vibrating differently as it passes. The figure puts numbers on this for 500 Hz: at 34.3 m/s a listener ahead hears 556 Hz and a listener behind hears 455 Hz, and at half the speed of sound the figures are 1000 Hz and 333 Hz.

diagram.alt: Three sets of circular wave fronts around a moving source, drawn as the source reaches the middle. When the source is at rest the circles are evenly spaced. As it moves right they crowd together ahead of it and spread out behind it.
diagram.caption: Wave fronts sent out at equal time steps by a 500 Hz source. Use the buttons to change the speed of the source.

steps.headline: A 600 Hz siren approaches a still listener at 34.3 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. Find the frequency heard.

workedSteps.text: The source approaches, so the wavelength in front is shortened and the denominator is v minus the source speed.
Work out the denominator.
The listener hears the source frequency multiplied by the ratio of v to this denominator.

steps.headline: The same siren drives away from the listener at 34.3 m/s. Find the frequency heard.

workedSteps.text: The source recedes, so the wavelength is stretched and the denominator is v plus the source speed.
Work out the denominator.
The listener hears the source frequency multiplied by the ratio of v to this denominator.

lead.text: If the source stands still and the listener walks towards it at v_o, the wavelength in the air is unchanged, but the listener meets the wave fronts faster, at v + v_o. The frequency received is *f' = f (v + v_o)/v*. A listener approaching a 500 Hz source at 34.3 m/s therefore hears 500 × (343 + 34.3)/343 = 550 Hz, which is lower than the 556 Hz heard when the *source* approaches at the same speed.

afterFigure.text: For small speeds the two answers are nearly equal, and the difference grows as the speed approaches that of sound.

reveal.text: You hear 529 Hz. Here the listener moves and the wavelength is unchanged, so the formula has the speed on top.
The pavement listener is at rest and the source moves, so the shortened wavelength applies.

lessons.orientation: Use the decibel scale and the Doppler shift.
lessons.nextAction: Follow light across the boundary between air and glass and see why it bends.

blocks.text: A sound just loud enough to hear has an intensity of about 10⁻¹² W/m², and a sound at the threshold of pain carries about 1 W/m², a trillion times more. No ordinary scale could hold both without most of its numbers being nearly meaningless, which is why sound is described by a logarithm, the decibel scale on which a sound meter reads.
Pitch has numbers attached as well, and they lead to a second calculation, of the frequency that reaches your ear from a source that is moving, such as the siren on an ambulance.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to convert intensity to decibels, add sources in decibels and calculate the frequency heard from a moving source or listener.
intro.whyItMatters: Both tools turn up well outside sound, in the ratings of electronics and in the redshift of starlight.

recap.keyIdea: Sound level is 10 log₁₀(I/I₀), so each factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB, and a moving source or listener changes the frequency received, as in f' = f v/(v − vₛ).

blocks.text: The decibel scale uses a logarithm to fit a trillion-fold range of intensities onto 0 to 120 dB, so doubling the intensity adds 3 dB and ten times the intensity adds 10 dB. A source that moves towards a listener crowds its wave fronts together and raises the frequency received, while a source that recedes stretches them and lowers it.
The source emits the same frequency throughout, and a moving listener gives a different formula from a moving source.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows light as it passes from air into glass, where its speed changes and its path bends.

lessons.title: Why light bends

reveal.text: The ray bends towards the normal, since the glass slows it. The next screen shows why a change of speed turns the ray, and the rule that says by how much comes after it.

lead.text: Light moves at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum and more slowly in a material. The ratio c/v is the material's **refractive index**, n, so that v = c/n: air has n of about 1.00, water 1.33 and common glass 1.50, which puts the speed in glass at 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.50 = 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s. The frequency is fixed by the source, so by v = fλ the wavelength in the glass is shorter by the same factor.

Now let a beam arrive at an angle. The part of a wavefront that reaches the glass first slows first, while the rest is still travelling at full speed in the air, so the front pivots about the edge of the surface. The ray, which is perpendicular to the wavefronts, turns with it, and the bending is called **refraction**.

afterFigure.text: A beam that arrives at 30° to the normal leaves the surface at 19.5° to the normal inside the glass, nearer to the normal than before. A beam travelling along the normal reaches the whole surface at once, so it is not turned at all, but its wavefronts still crowd together as it slows.

diagram.alt: Wavefronts crossing a boundary between air and glass. At 30 degrees, evenly spaced wavefronts in the air become more closely spaced in the glass and turn towards the normal. For a ray at 0 degrees the wavefronts stay parallel to the surface and crowd together.
diagram.caption: Wavefronts spaced one wavelength apart: 60 units in air, 40 in glass, because light moves at two thirds of its speed in glass.

reveal.text: Light travels at 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s inside diamond, about 41% of its vacuum speed, which is slower than in any common glass.

lead.text: The turning of the ray follows a precise rule. If the ray makes an angle θ₁ with the normal in a medium of index n₁ and θ₂ in a medium of index n₂, then *n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂*, known as **Snell's law**. Here the [[sine|In a right triangle, the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. Met in the Trigonometry course.]] of an angle can be found on a calculator, and the inverse operation, arcsin, finds the angle from its sine.

Both angles are measured from the normal, never from the surface, and the larger index goes with the smaller angle: **light entering a higher index bends towards the normal, and light entering a lower index bends away from it**.

afterFigure.text: Air to glass at 30° gives sin θ₂ = 1.00 × sin 30° / 1.50 = 0.333, so θ₂ = 19.5°. Glass to air at the same 30° gives sin θ₂ = 1.50 × 0.500 = 0.750 and θ₂ = 48.6°, bent away from the normal. Along the normal, sin 0° = 0 on both sides, so the angle stays at 0°.

diagram.alt: Rays crossing a boundary between air and glass, with the normal drawn as a dashed vertical line. Air to glass at 30 degrees bends towards the normal to 19.5 degrees; glass to air at 30 degrees bends away from it to 48.6 degrees; a ray along the normal does not bend.
diagram.caption: Angles are measured from the normal, not from the surface. Use the buttons to compare the three crossings.

steps.headline: A ray in air meets glass of index 1.50 at 45° to the normal. Find the angle of the ray in the glass.

workedSteps.text: Write Snell's law, with medium 1 as air and medium 2 as glass.
workedSteps.math: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂

workedSteps.text: Solve for the sine of the new angle and substitute, using sin 45° = 0.707.
That gives the sine of the new angle.
Take the arcsine to find the angle.

steps.headline: A ray in air meets water, of index 1.33, at 40° to the normal. Find its angle in the water.

workedSteps.text: Write Snell's law and solve for sin θ₂.
Substitute, using sin 40° = 0.643.
The angle is the inverse sine of that value.

lead.text: Reverse the journey, so that light inside glass meets the surface to air. Now the ray bends *away* from the normal, and as the incident angle grows the refracted angle grows faster, until the refracted ray skims along the surface at 90°. That incident angle is the **critical angle**, found by putting sin θ₂ = 1 in Snell's law: *sin θ_c = n₂/n₁*. For glass to air, θ_c = arcsin(1.00/1.50) = 41.8°.

afterFigure.text: Beyond 41.8° no solution exists, because n₁ sin θ₁ would need a sine larger than 1, and none of the light leaves. All of it is reflected back into the glass, a result called **total internal reflection**, shown in the last case of the figure. It occurs only in the direction from the higher index to the lower. Fibre-optic cables rely on it, for the light inside a thin glass strand meets the walls at angles beyond the critical angle and is carried along the strand.

diagram.alt: Rays inside glass meeting the surface to air at three angles of incidence: 30 degrees, where the ray leaves bent away from the normal to 48.6 degrees; 41.8 degrees, the critical angle, where it leaves along the surface; and 50 degrees, where it is entirely reflected.
diagram.caption: Light inside glass meeting a glass-air surface. Above the critical angle of 41.8° nothing leaves. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Above this angle none of the light escapes upwards, which is why a diver looking up sees a bright circle with a mirror-like surround.

lead.text: The value of n for a given material is not quite the same for every colour: in glass, blue light is slowed a little more than red light. By Snell's law blue is therefore bent through a larger angle than red, so a beam of white light entering a prism at an angle leaves as a spread of colours, a result called **dispersion**. Raindrops do the same thing with sunlight on a larger scale and in combination with total internal reflection, which makes a rainbow.

The difference in index between red and blue light is less than one percent in ordinary glass, but a prism has two tilted surfaces, and the small difference in the angle at each is enough to fan the colours out.

reveal.text: The ray leaves into the air at a larger angle to the normal, because it is going from the higher index to the lower. Both angles are measured from the normal.

lessons.orientation: Apply Snell's law and find a critical angle.
lessons.nextAction: Use curved glass to focus light and to place an image.

blocks.text: Light travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum and at only 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s in ordinary glass, and that change of speed at the surface is why a straight stick looks bent where it enters water and why a glass prism spreads white light into colours. A beam that meets the surface at an angle changes direction as it crosses.

One equation gives the new direction from the old. The same equation explains why, at a steep enough angle, light inside glass or water cannot leave at all, which is what keeps light inside an optical fibre along its whole length.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use Snell's law to find a refracted angle and a critical angle.
intro.whyItMatters: Every lens, from a camera to your own eye, works by refraction.

recap.keyIdea: Light bends at a boundary because its speed changes, following n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, and beyond the critical angle sin θ_c = n₂/n₁ it reflects completely.

blocks.text: Light slows to c/n in a material, and a wavefront that arrives at an angle turns because one end slows first. Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, gives the new angle measured from the normal, towards it when the index rises and away from it when the index falls.

Going from a higher index to a lower one there is a critical angle, arcsin(n₂/n₁), beyond which all of the light reflects, and because n varies a little with wavelength, a prism also spreads white light into colours.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shapes glass into lenses, so that refraction at two curved surfaces gathers light to form images.

lessons.title: Lenses and images

lead.text: A lens whose middle is thicker than its edges refracts every ray towards the axis, and so a bundle of parallel rays leaves it heading to a single spot on the axis called the **focal point**. The distance from the lens to that spot is the **focal length**, f, and a lens of this kind is called a **converging lens**. Light can enter from either side, so a lens has a focal point on each side, both at the distance f.

To find the image of the top of an object, follow the three rays whose paths can be drawn exactly. A ray travelling parallel to the axis leaves through the far focal point. A ray through the centre of the thin lens passes on in a straight line. A ray that travels through the near focal point leaves parallel to the axis. Where the three meet again is the image of that point.

afterFigure.text: In the figure f = 10 cm and the object is 30 cm from the lens. The three rays meet 15 cm beyond the lens, below the axis, so the image is upside down and smaller. Moving the object to 15 cm sends the image out to 30 cm and makes it larger, as the second button shows: the nearer the object comes to the lens, the farther away its image forms.

diagram.alt: A converging lens with focal length 10 cm. An object 5 cm tall stands 30 cm away in one case and 15 cm away in the other. Three rays from the top of the object meet again at the image, which is upside down.
diagram.caption: Three rays from the top of the object: parallel to the axis (orange), through the centre (green) and through the near focal point (blue). Use the buttons to move the object.

reveal.text: The image forms 20 cm on the other side, the same distance as the object, and the next screen gives the equation that predicts this.

lead.text: Measuring the distances from the lens, the object distance d_o, the image distance d_i and the focal length f are related by the **thin-lens equation**, *1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i*. The size of the image compared with the size of the object is the **magnification**, *m = −d_i/d_o*, so that the height of the image is m times the height of the object.

The signs carry meaning. A positive d_i places the image on the far side of the lens, where the rays really cross, and a negative d_i places it on the near side. A negative m means the image is **inverted**, upside down, and a positive m means it is upright. **The size of the image is the absolute value of m**, so m = −0.5 means half size and upside down, not smaller by a minus sign.
For f = 10 cm and d_o = 30 cm, 1/d_i = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so d_i = 15 cm, and m = −15/30 = −0.5. The image is upside down and half the height of the object.

steps.headline: A lens of focal length 10 cm forms an image of an object 60 cm away. Find the image distance and the magnification.

workedSteps.text: Write the thin-lens equation and rearrange it for the image distance.
Substitute the focal length and the object distance.
The image distance is the reciprocal of that difference.
Now the magnification, with the image distance just found.

steps.headline: A lens of focal length 15 cm forms an image of an object 45 cm away. Find the image distance and the magnification.

workedSteps.text: Rearrange the thin-lens equation.
Substitute the focal length and the object distance.
The image distance is the reciprocal of that difference.
The magnification follows from the image distance just found.

lead.text: When the object is farther from the lens than the focal length, the rays leave the lens heading towards one another and actually cross, and a screen placed there shows the image. This is a **real image**. When the object is closer than the focal length, the lens cannot bend the rays enough to bring them together, and they leave still spreading apart, so that they only *appear* to come from a point on the object's side of the lens. This is a **virtual image**.

For f = 10 cm and an object at 5 cm, 1/d_i = 1/10 − 1/5 = −1/10, so d_i = −10 cm and m = −(−10)/5 = +2. The negative image distance says the image is on the same side as the object, and the positive magnification says it is upright and twice the height.

afterFigure.text: The eye sees it, because the eye only needs rays that diverge from a point, but no screen placed there would catch anything. A **magnifying glass** is a converging lens held with the object inside its focal length, and it works by producing a larger, upright, virtual image.

diagram.alt: A converging lens with focal length 10 cm and an object 5 cm away, closer than the focal length. The three rays spread out after the lens, and the image is where they appear to come from, behind the object, upright and twice as tall.

reveal.text: The image is virtual, upright and larger, which is why a magnifying glass is held close to the page.
The negative sign marks a virtual image on the same side of the lens as the object.

lead.text: The lens of a camera and the lens and cornea of your eye are converging systems that form a real, inverted image of what they look at on the sensor or the retina. To focus on a nearer object the image distance must grow, and a camera does this by moving the lens slightly away from the sensor, while the eye does it by changing the shape of its lens.
An image upside down on the retina is turned the right way up by the brain.

reveal.text: The sensor must be a little more than 50 mm from the lens, which is why a lens moves outwards to focus on nearby objects.

lessons.orientation: Locate an image with the thin-lens equation and describe it.
lessons.nextAction: Move from light to electricity, starting with charge and the force between charges.

blocks.text: A converging lens with a focal length of 10 cm, held 30 cm from a lamp, puts a sharp image of the lamp on a card 15 cm behind it, upside down and half the size. Hold the lamp 5 cm from the lens instead and no position of the card gives a sharp image, though looking through the lens shows a lamp twice as large and the right way up. The two results follow from one equation, and the difference between them separates a real image from a virtual one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the image distance and magnification for a thin lens, and say whether the image is real or virtual, upright or inverted.
intro.whyItMatters: Cameras, spectacles and microscopes are all built from the same equation.

recap.keyIdea: For a thin lens 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i and m = −d_i/d_o: a positive d_i is a real image, a negative m is an inverted one.

blocks.text: Three rays from the top of an object locate its image, and the thin-lens equation does the same job with numbers. An object beyond the focal length gives a real image that can be caught on a screen, normally inverted, while an object inside the focal length gives a virtual, upright, larger image that the eye sees but no screen catches.
The signs of d_i and m carry that information, and the size of the image is always the absolute value of m.

lessons.title: Charge and the force between charges

reveal.text: The paper pieces are attracted, though they have no net charge. The next screen explains how a charged object can pull on something neutral.

lead.text: Charge comes in two kinds, called positive and negative. Two objects with charge of the same sign push each other apart, and two with opposite signs pull together. The forces on the two objects are equal in size and opposite in direction, as they must be by Newton's third law. The unit of charge is the **coulomb** (C), and the smallest free charge is that of an electron or a proton, the **elementary charge** *e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C*, negative for the electron and positive for the proton.

Rubbing a balloon on wool does not create charge. It moves electrons from one material to the other, so that the wool is left with too few and the balloon with too many, and the two charges are equal and opposite. **The total charge never changes**, which is what *conservation of charge* means.

afterFigure.text: A neutral object has equal amounts of positive and negative charge, and in a conductor or in paper the negative charges can shift a little. A charged balloon therefore pulls the nearer charges of the paper towards it and pushes the farther ones away, and since the nearer side is closer the pull wins. This is **polarisation**, and it is why a charged object attracts neutral ones.

diagram.alt: Two charged balls with arrows showing the forces on them. Two positive balls are pushed apart, two negative balls are pushed apart, and a positive and a negative ball are pulled together.
diagram.caption: The force on each charge, drawn as an arrow. Use the buttons to change the signs.

reveal.text: About six million million electrons made the transfer, a tiny fraction of the electrons in the rod, which is why rubbing leaves a rod looking unchanged.

lead.text: The size of the force between two small charged objects, q₁ and q₂, separated by a distance r, is given by **Coulomb's law**: *F = k q₁ q₂ / r²*, where k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C². The force acts along the line joining the charges. The charges are in coulombs and the separation in metres, which gives the force in newtons.

A coulomb is a very large charge, and the charges met in the laboratory are microcoulombs, 10⁻⁶ C. Two charges of 1.0 µC at a separation of 0.10 m give F = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (1.0 × 10⁻⁶)² / (0.10)² = 0.899 N, which is the weight of a mass of about 90 g.

afterFigure.text: The force is large when the charges are close and drops quickly: at 0.20 m, twice the distance, the same charges give only 0.225 N, a quarter of the previous value.

diagram.alt: A graph of the force between two 1.0 microcoulomb charges against their separation, falling steeply from 3.6 newtons at 0.05 metres to 0.056 newtons at 0.40 metres. The force at 0.20 metres is a quarter of the force at 0.10 metres.
diagram.caption: Doubling the separation, from 0.10 m to 0.20 m, cuts the force from 0.899 N to 0.225 N.

steps.headline: Two charges of 2.0 µC are 0.30 m apart. Find the size of the force between them.

workedSteps.text: Write Coulomb's law.
Convert the charges to coulombs and substitute.
Work out the square of the separation.
Now the whole calculation: the top is 8.99 × 10⁹ × 4.0 × 10⁻¹² = 3.60 × 10⁻² and the bottom is 0.090.
Both charges are positive, so the force is a repulsion.

reveal.text: The force falls to one ninth of its original value, not one third. The next screen explains why a factor of 3 in distance gives a factor of 9 in force.

lead.text: Because F depends on 1/r², any change of the separation by a factor n changes the force by 1/n². Doubling the distance gives a quarter of the force, tripling it a ninth, and halving it four times the force. This is an **inverse-square law**, and Newton's law of gravitation, with its [[inverse-square form|F = G m₁ m₂ / r², met in Physics: Motion and Forces.]], has the same shape, with masses in place of charges.

The two forces differ enormously in size. Two protons repel with F = k e² / r² and attract through gravity with G m² / r², and the distance cancels from the ratio, so the ratio is k e² / (G m²) = 8.99 × 10⁹ × (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹)² / (6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ × (1.673 × 10⁻²⁷)²) ≈ 1.2 × 10³⁶.

afterFigure.text: Gravity is nevertheless the force that governs planets, because large objects are nearly neutral, so that the electric forces of their positive and negative charges cancel while gravity only ever adds.

steps.headline: A 3.0 µC charge and a −2.0 µC charge are 0.15 m apart. Find the size and direction of the force.

workedSteps.text: Write Coulomb's law and use the sizes of the charges.
The product of the charges is needed in coulombs squared, with the sign ignored.
The force follows from k, this product and the square of the separation.
The signs are opposite, so the force is an attraction.

reveal.text: The force is a ninth of 0.899 N, which is 0.100 N, so tripling the separation has cut the force by almost 90%.
The attraction of 8.2 × 10⁻⁸ N is tiny in everyday terms, but it acts on an electron of mass only 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, and that is enough to hold the atom together.

lessons.orientation: Calculate the force between point charges with Coulomb's law.
lessons.reviewLabel: Charge and the force between charges
lessons.nextAction: Describe the space around a charge with the electric field, and measure the energy of charge with voltage.

blocks.text: Two charges of 1.0 µC, 0.10 m apart, push on each other with a force of 0.899 N, about the weight of a 90 g mass, while the same two charges 1 mm apart would push with 9 kN, about the weight of a small car. Bringing the charges a hundred times closer has made the force ten thousand times larger, and that steep rise is the first sign of the rule that governs every electric force.
The rule is a single equation, **Coulomb's law**, which has the same shape as Newton's law of gravitation.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use Coulomb's law to find the force between two charges and to say how it changes when the distance changes.
intro.whyItMatters: The rest of the electrical lessons are built on this one force law.

recap.keyIdea: The force between two point charges is F = k q₁q₂/r², attractive for unlike charges and repulsive for like ones, and it falls to a quarter when the distance doubles.

blocks.text: Charge has two signs, is moved and never created, and is measured in coulombs. Coulomb's law gives the force between two small charged objects as k q₁q₂/r² with k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², so doubling the separation divides the force by 4 and tripling it divides it by 9.
The law has the same shape as gravity, but between two protons the electric force is about 10³⁶ times larger.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson describes the space around a charge as an electric field, and introduces voltage.

lessons.title: Fields and voltage

lead.text: Place a small test charge q at a point and measure the force F on it, and the quotient *E = F/q* is the **electric field** at that point: the force that each coulomb of charge would feel there. It is a vector, and its direction is the direction of the force on a *positive* test charge. Its unit is the newton per coulomb, N/C.
For a point charge Q, Coulomb's law gives a force kQq/r² on the test charge, so the field is *E = kQ/r²*. At 0.50 m from a charge of 2.0 µC it is 8.99 × 10⁹ × 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ / 0.50² = 7.2 × 10⁴ N/C.

afterFigure.text: The arrows point away from a positive charge and towards a negative one, and they shorten with distance because the field falls as 1/r². Arrows and the field lines drawn through them show the direction of the *force* at each point, not the path that a charge follows: a charge released from rest starts to move along them but may curve away if it had any velocity.

diagram.alt: Arrows showing the electric field of a single point charge at two distances. For a positive charge the arrows point away from it and for a negative charge they point towards it. The arrows are longer near the charge, where the field is stronger.

reveal.text: The field at that point is 3.0 × 10⁴ N/C, in the direction of the force if the test charge is positive.
The field halves, because the same 12 V is spread over twice the distance. The next screen shows this as E = V/d.

lead.text: Moving a charge against the field takes work, and moving it along the field releases energy. The **potential difference**, or **voltage**, between two points is the energy gained per unit of charge in going from one to the other, *V = ΔE/q*, and its unit is the volt, V, which is a joule per coulomb. A 12 V battery maintains 12 V between its terminals, so that every coulomb that passes from one terminal to the other changes its energy by 12 J. Voltage is not something that flows: charge flows, and the voltage is the difference in energy per charge that drives it.

Between two parallel plates the field is uniform, with the same strength and direction everywhere in the gap. The energy per charge changes steadily across the gap, and over a gap d with a voltage V across it the field is *E = V/d*.

afterFigure.text: The dashed lines in the figure join points at the same voltage, and with 12 V across 0.020 m the field is 12 / 0.020 = 600 V/m. With the plates 0.040 m apart the field falls to 300 V/m, and the dashed lines spread out. The units V/m and N/C are the same unit, since a volt is a joule per coulomb and a joule is a newton metre.

reveal.text: The field is 240 V/m, the same in every part of the gap.

lead.text: Since a volt is a joule per coulomb, a charge q that moves through a potential difference V gains the energy *ΔE = qV*. A charge of 2.0 C crossing 1.5 V gains 3.0 J. For a single electron the charge is only 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and the energy gained through 1 V is called one **electron-volt**, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, a unit suited to atoms. An electron that crosses 250 V gains 250 eV.

If the charge starts at rest and nothing else takes energy, the gain appears as [[kinetic energy|The energy of motion, ½mv². Met in Physics: Motion and Forces.]], so qV = ½mv² and the speed is *v = √(2qV/m)*.

afterFigure.text: The mass of the electron, 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg, is so small that a modest voltage gives it a speed that is a sizeable fraction of the speed of light.

steps.headline: An electron, starting at rest, is accelerated across a potential difference of 100 V. Find the energy it gains and its final speed.

workedSteps.text: The energy gained is the charge times the voltage. In electron-volts this is just the voltage, 100 eV; in joules, use the electron charge.
All of it becomes kinetic energy, so set it equal to ½mv² and solve for v.
Substitute the energy and the electron mass into the fraction under the root.
The speed is the square root of that fraction.

steps.headline: A proton, starting at rest, is accelerated across 500 V. Find its final speed. The proton mass is 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

workedSteps.text: The energy gained is qV, with the proton charge 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Set the energy equal to ½mv² and solve for v.
The fraction under the root works out to 9.58 × 10¹⁰ m²/s².

reveal.text: The ion gains 500 eV, 1 eV per volt for each of its two elementary charges, and that simple counting is what makes the unit convenient.
The force is tiny in newtons, but on an electron of mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg it gives an enormous acceleration of about 10¹⁴ m/s².

lessons.orientation: Use field and voltage to find forces and speeds of charges.
lessons.nextAction: See how a charge moving through a magnetic field feels a force at right angles to its motion.

blocks.text: A 12 V battery joined to two metal plates 0.020 m apart fills the gap between them with a steady push on any charge placed there, the same in strength and direction at every point. An electron let go beside the negative plate is driven across the gap, and by the time it reaches the other side it has gained an amount of energy set by the battery's 12 V alone, whatever the width of the gap.

Two quantities describe this: the **electric field**, which is the force that each coulomb of charge would feel at a point, and the **voltage** between two points, which is the energy each coulomb gains in moving from one to the other and is the number printed on a battery.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the field between plates, the energy a charge gains from a voltage and the speed it reaches.
intro.whyItMatters: These two ideas turn the force law of the last lesson into something you can set up with a battery.

recap.keyIdea: The field is E = F/q, between plates E = V/d, and a charge q crossing a voltage V gains energy qV.

blocks.text: The electric field is the force per unit charge, and the voltage is the energy per unit charge, so the field between parallel plates is the voltage divided by the gap. A charge that crosses a voltage V gains qV of energy, which for an electron is measured in electron-volts, and setting this equal to ½mv² gives its speed.
Charge flows, and voltage is the difference in energy per charge that drives the flow.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns to a charge that is already moving, which feels a different force, one at right angles to its velocity.

lessons.title: Magnetic force

reveal.text: The speed stays at 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s: the force is always at right angles to the motion, so it turns the proton without speeding it up or slowing it down.

lead.text: Around a magnet there is a **magnetic field**, B, whose unit is the tesla (T). The field of the Earth at the surface is about 5 × 10⁻⁵ T, and a strong laboratory magnet gives about 1 T. A charge at rest feels no magnetic force at all. A charge q moving with velocity v through a field B feels a force of size *F = q v B sin θ*, where θ is the angle between v and B, so only the part of the velocity *across* the field counts and a charge moving along the field is not pushed.

The direction of the force is at right angles to both v and B, and for a positive charge it follows the **right-hand rule**: point the fingers of the right hand along v, curl them towards B, and the thumb gives F. In the figure the field points into the page and the charge moves right, so the force on a positive charge is up and, with the sign of the charge reversed, down.

afterFigure.text: The force is not along the field, as an electric force would be, and it never has a component along the velocity. A force at right angles to the motion does no work on the charge, so **it changes the direction of the velocity but not the speed**.

diagram.alt: A charge moving to the right through a magnetic field pointing into the page. A positive charge feels a force upward, perpendicular to its velocity and to the field; a negative charge feels the same force downward.
diagram.caption: Velocity v, field B and force F for a positive and a negative charge. Use the buttons to change the sign.

lead.text: Because the force always points at right angles to the velocity, with constant size, it supplies exactly the [[centripetal force|The inward force that keeps an object moving in a circle, mv²/r. Met in Physics: Motion and Forces.]] for a circular path, and the charge moves around a circle at constant speed. Setting the magnetic force equal to the centripetal force, qvB = mv²/r, gives *r = mv/(qB)*.
A positive charge circles in the sense of the force in the figure, anticlockwise for a field into the page, and a negative charge circles the other way.

afterFigure.text: For the electron of the last screen, r = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × 1.0 × 10⁶ / (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.010) = 5.7 × 10⁻⁴ m, about half a millimetre. Doubling the speed doubles the radius, and the figure shows the larger circle. **The time for one circuit does not depend on the speed**, since the circumference grows in step with the speed, and that fact is what a cyclotron uses to accelerate particles.

reveal.text: The radius grows six times, since r is proportional to v and inversely proportional to B, and the time for a full circle doubles because it depends on the field but not on the speed.

steps.headline: An electron moves at 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a field of 0.020 T. Find the radius of its circular path.

workedSteps.text: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force.
Substitute the electron's mass and charge.
The top works out to 2.733 × 10⁻²⁴ and the bottom to 3.204 × 10⁻²¹.
That is 0.85 mm, a circle smaller than a grain of rice.

steps.headline: A proton moves at 2.0 × 10⁶ m/s at right angles to a field of 0.50 T. Find the radius of its path. The proton mass is 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ kg.

workedSteps.text: Use the same relation as before.
Substitute the values.
The fraction gives the radius in metres.

lead.text: A current is charge in motion, so a wire carrying a current in a magnetic field feels the sum of the forces on its moving charges. For a straight length L of wire carrying a current I at an angle θ to the field, *F = B I L sin θ*, and the force is perpendicular to both the wire and the field.
For the numbers shown, B = 0.50 T, I = 4.0 A and L = 0.25 m across the field gives F = 0.50 × 4.0 × 0.25 = 0.50 N.

afterFigure.text: This force is how an electric motor works: a coil of wire carrying a current sits in a magnetic field, the forces on its two sides act in opposite directions and turn the coil, and a switching of the current keeps the turning going.

diagram.alt: A straight wire carrying current across a magnetic field that points into the page. With the current to the right the force on the wire is upward; reversing the current reverses the force.
diagram.caption: A current is moving charge, so the wire feels the sum of the forces on its charges. Use the buttons to reverse the current.

reveal.text: The force is 0.24 N, acting at right angles to both the wire and the field.
Only the component of the wire across the field matters, and sin 30° = 0.5, so the force is half what it would be at right angles.

lessons.orientation: Find the magnetic force on moving charges and currents, and the radius of a circular path.
lessons.nextAction: Find out how a changing magnetic field produces a voltage, and use it in a transformer.

blocks.text: A beam of electrons crossing a magnetic field at right angles curves round into a circle, and in a field of 0.010 T an electron moving at 1.0 × 10⁶ m/s follows a circle only 0.57 mm in radius. The push that bends it acts sideways, at right angles both to the field and to the electron's motion, which makes it quite unlike the push of one charge on another, since that acts along the line between them.
One rule gives the size and direction of that sideways push on a moving charge, and the same rule, applied to the charges moving along a wire, gives the force on the wire.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the magnetic force on a moving charge and on a wire, and the radius of a charge's circular path.
intro.whyItMatters: Motors, loudspeakers and particle accelerators rely on this force.

recap.keyIdea: A moving charge feels F = qvB sin θ at right angles to both v and B, which bends its path into a circle of radius mv/(qB), and a wire feels F = BIL sin θ.

blocks.text: A magnetic field acts only on moving charges, with a force F = qvB sin θ that points at right angles to both the velocity and the field, so it turns a charge without changing its speed. A charge crossing the field at right angles follows a circle of radius mv/(qB), and a wire carrying current I across the field feels F = BIL.
Doubling the speed doubles the radius, and the angle in sin θ is the angle between the motion and the field.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson shows what happens when a magnetic field changes, which can drive a current and is the basis of the transformer.

lessons.title: Changing fields make voltage

reveal.text: The meter reads zero. A voltage appears only while the field through the coil is changing, however strong the magnet may be.

lead.text: Push the north pole of a magnet towards a coil connected to a sensitive meter and the needle kicks; hold the magnet still and the needle returns to zero; pull the magnet back and the needle kicks the other way. Nothing about the magnet's strength accounts for this, since the same magnet gives zero when it is held still, so what the coil responds to is a *change* in the magnetic field passing through it. The voltage this produces is called an induced **emf**.

To measure the change we need a quantity for the amount of field through the coil. A coil of area A in a uniform field B has **magnetic flux** *Φ = B A cos θ*, where θ is the angle between the field and the line at right angles to the coil. The unit of flux is the weber, Wb, equal to one tesla metre squared.

afterFigure.text: A field at right angles to the coil, θ = 0, gives the greatest flux, and one running along the coil's surface, θ = 90°, gives none, since cos 90° = 0. A field of 0.50 T through a coil of area 0.010 m² has a flux of 0.50 × 0.010 = 0.0050 Wb.

diagram.alt: A bar magnet and a coil of wire joined to a meter. Pushing the magnet into the coil makes the needle kick one way, pulling it out makes the needle kick the other way, and leaving it at rest inside the coil gives no reading.
diagram.caption: The needle moves only while the magnet moves. Use the buttons to compare the three cases.

reveal.text: The flux is half of the largest value it could have, because cos 60° = 0.5.

lead.text: The faster the flux changes, the larger the induced emf, and a coil of N turns, each linked by the same flux, adds up the emf of every turn. **Faraday's law** says *emf = N ΔΦ/Δt* in size: the number of turns times the change in flux divided by the time taken. In the figure the flux through a coil of 100 turns rises by 0.0050 Wb in 0.20 s, which gives 100 × 0.0050 / 0.20 = 2.5 V, and the same rise over 0.40 s gives only 1.25 V.

A steady flux has a slope of zero on the graph and so induces nothing, whatever its size, which is the case of the magnet held still. **It is the rate of change that matters, and not the amount of flux.**

afterFigure.text: The direction of the emf follows **Lenz's law**: the current it drives makes a magnetic field that opposes the change in the flux. A magnet pushed towards a coil is repelled by the current it induces, so the person pushing must do work, and that work is the energy that appears in the circuit. The law is why induction does not create energy; without the opposition the magnet would be pulled in with ever more force, and energy would come from nothing.

steps.headline: A coil of 200 turns and area 0.020 m² has a field of 0.30 T switched on at right angles to it, rising from 0 to 0.30 T in 0.15 s. Find the induced emf.

workedSteps.text: The flux through the coil changes from zero to BA, since the field is at right angles to the coil.
Faraday's law then gives the emf from N = 200 turns, this change in flux and a time of 0.15 s.
By Lenz's law the current in the coil would make a field that opposes the increase.

steps.headline: A coil of 250 turns and area 0.020 m² loses a 0.80 T field in 0.050 s. Find the induced emf.

workedSteps.text: The flux changes by BA, from 0.80 × 0.020 to zero.
Faraday's law with N = 250 and Δt = 0.050 s gives the emf.

lead.text: Spin a coil in a uniform field and the angle θ between the field and the coil's axis keeps changing, so the flux BA cos θ rises to a maximum, falls through zero, reverses and returns, once for each turn. The flux is changing all the time, so there is an emf all the time, and its direction reverses twice in every turn. This is a **generator**, and the emf is an alternating sine wave of peak value *N B A ω*, where ω = 2πf is the rate of turning in radians per second and f the number of turns per second.

afterFigure.text: Mains electricity is generated in this way, by large coils spun in power stations, and the supply alternates because the emf does. Its frequency is 50 Hz in Europe and 60 Hz in North America, the rate at which the generators turn.

diagram.alt: A sine wave of emf against time with a peak of 157 volts and a period of 0.020 seconds, the output of a coil of 100 turns and area 0.010 square metres spun at 50 hertz in a field of 0.50 tesla.
diagram.caption: A spinning coil gives an emf that alternates, 157 V at the peak, repeating 50 times a second.

reveal.text: The output is 11.5 V, which is the input voltage multiplied by the ratio of the turns, 50 / 1000. The next screen shows why.

lead.text: Two coils wound on one iron core share the same changing flux. A changing current in the input, or primary, coil of N_p turns sets up a changing flux in the core, and this induces an emf in each turn of the output, or secondary, coil of N_s turns, so that *V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p*. It needs a changing flux, so a transformer works only with **alternating current**, and a steady direct current in the primary induces nothing in the secondary.

A transformer does not make energy. In the ideal case the output power equals the input power, V_p I_p = V_s I_s, so a transformer that steps the voltage up steps the current down by the same factor, and the reverse.

afterFigure.text: This is why electricity is sent over long distances at a very high voltage. To deliver 100 kW at 230 V needs a current of 435 A, and a line of resistance 0.10 Ω would lose I²R = 435² × 0.10 = 18.9 kW as heat. At 23 000 V the same power needs only 4.35 A, and the loss falls to 4.35² × 0.10 = 1.89 W, a ten-thousandth as much.

diagram.alt: A transformer with two coils wound on an iron core. With 1000 turns on the input side and 50 on the output side, 230 volts in gives 11.5 volts out. Reversing the turns, 50 in and 1000 out, steps 230 volts up to 4600 volts.
diagram.caption: Two coils on one iron core. The output voltage is the input voltage times the ratio of the turns. Use the buttons to swap the turns.
