lessons.orientation: Apply Faraday's law and the transformer rule.
lessons.nextAction: Put these ideas together to see that a changing electric and magnetic field can travel as a wave of light.

blocks.text: Push a magnet into a coil of wire joined to a sensitive meter and the needle kicks, and pull the magnet out again and it kicks the other way, although nothing touches the wire and there is no battery anywhere in the circuit. The moving magnet has produced a voltage in the coil, an effect that Michael Faraday discovered in 1831.

Nearly all of the world's electricity is generated in this way, by turning coils inside magnetic fields, and the same effect lets a transformer change an alternating voltage, stepping 230 V down to a few volts or up to many thousands for a long transmission line.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the emf induced by a changing flux and the output voltage of a transformer.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost all of the world's electricity is generated by induction and distributed through transformers.

recap.keyIdea: A changing flux induces an emf of N ΔΦ/Δt, and a transformer scales an alternating voltage in the ratio of its turns, Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.

blocks.text: The flux through a coil is BA cos θ, and a change in it, not its size, induces an emf of N ΔΦ/Δt that acts to oppose the change, as Lenz's law requires. A coil spinning in a field gives an alternating emf, and a transformer, working on the changing flux in an iron core, multiplies an alternating voltage by the ratio of the turns.
Because the power is the same on both sides, raising the voltage lowers the current, which is why power is sent along transmission lines at a high voltage.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson combines changing electric and magnetic fields and finds that together they travel through space as light.

lessons.title: Light as an electromagnetic wave

reveal.text: Light needs no material at all. It crosses a vacuum because it is carried by electric and magnetic fields, which exist in empty space.

lead.text: The last lesson showed that a changing magnetic field produces an electric field, which is the emf driving the current in a coil. James Clerk Maxwell, in the 1860s, completed the picture by adding that the reverse also holds: **a changing electric field produces a magnetic field**. Each of the two fields, while it changes, makes the other.

Together this gives a loop with no need for charges or wires. A changing electric field creates a magnetic field, which because it is changing creates an electric field a little further on, and so on, so that the disturbance moves outward through space as an **electromagnetic wave**. In the figure the two fields oscillate at right angles to one another and to the direction of travel, which makes the wave transverse, and the pattern moves on as time passes.

afterFigure.text: Light, as well as radio waves and X-rays, is a wave of this kind.

diagram.alt: A wave drawn along an axis of travel. The electric field oscillates up and down and the magnetic field oscillates at right angles to it, both at right angles to the direction of travel. A quarter of a period later the whole pattern has moved a quarter of a wavelength to the right.
diagram.caption: The electric and magnetic fields of a light wave. Use the buttons to see the pattern move on a quarter of a period.

cases.label: A quarter of a period later

reveal.text: Light from the Moon is 1.28 s old when it reaches us, so you always see the Moon as it was a little over a second earlier.

lead.text: From the equations that link the two kinds of field, Maxwell worked out the speed of the wave. It depends on just two constants: ε₀, the constant behind Coulomb's law, where k = 1/(4πε₀), and μ₀, the constant behind the magnetic force between currents. The speed is *c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀)*, and with μ₀ = 1.257 × 10⁻⁶ and ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² in SI units this is 1/√(1.113 × 10⁻¹⁷) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

That is the measured speed of light. In 1865 Maxwell concluded that light is an electromagnetic wave, and in 1887 and 1888 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected radio waves in his laboratory and found that they travel at that speed too.

afterFigure.text: The speed of every electromagnetic wave in a vacuum is the same, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, whatever its frequency, so higher-frequency light does not travel faster. The time that light takes to cross a distance d is just d/c, which is how astronomers speak of a distance in light-minutes or light-years.

reveal.text: The light that you see from the Sun left it a little over eight minutes ago.

lead.text: Nothing in the argument fixed the frequency of the wave. Any frequency can be produced by shaking a charge at that rate, and the result is always a wave travelling at c, so the relation *c = fλ* ties every frequency to a wavelength. The whole range is called the **electromagnetic spectrum**.

From the longest wavelengths to the shortest, the bands are radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Visible light occupies only the narrow stretch from about 400 nm, which we see as violet, to about 700 nm, which we see as red.

afterFigure.text: The bands differ only in frequency, and so in how they interact with matter. A mobile phone signal of 1.8 GHz has a wavelength of 3.00 × 10⁸ / 1.8 × 10⁹ = 0.167 m, and an FM radio station of 100 MHz sends out waves of 3 m.

diagram.alt: A bar showing the electromagnetic spectrum from radio waves at 1 kilometre wavelength through microwaves, infrared, a narrow band of visible light, ultraviolet and X-rays to gamma rays at 1 picometre, with a frequency under each wavelength mark.
diagram.caption: Every band is the same kind of wave with a different wavelength. Visible light is only a very small part of the spectrum.

steps.headline: A microwave oven uses waves of frequency 2.45 GHz. Find their wavelength.

workedSteps.text: Convert the frequency to hertz. The prefix giga means 10⁹.
Rearranging c = fλ gives the wavelength as λ = c / f.
This wavelength, 12 cm, is smaller than the oven door.

steps.headline: An X-ray machine produces waves of wavelength 0.10 nm. Find their frequency.

workedSteps.text: Convert the wavelength to metres. The prefix nano means 10⁻⁹.
Rearranging c = fλ gives the frequency as f = c / λ.

lead.text: A light wave exchanges energy with matter in separate packets, called **photons**, and the energy of one photon is proportional to the frequency: *E = hf*, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is Planck's constant. For green light of 500 nm, f = 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and E = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ × 6.0 × 10¹⁴ = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, which is 2.5 eV, the size of the energy steps in atoms.

afterFigure.text: A photon of radio waves carries about a million times less energy than one of visible light and so can do nothing to an atom, while an X-ray photon of 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz carries enough to knock electrons out of atoms, which is why X-rays are used with care.

reveal.text: The shortest wavelength has the highest frequency, since in a vacuum f = c/λ for all of them.
Radio waves are electromagnetic waves too, so the signal travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, and a conversation with the rover has a delay of several minutes.

lessons.orientation: Connect changing fields to light and use the wave equation across the spectrum.
lessons.nextAction: Turn to heat, and the difference between heat and temperature.

blocks.text: Light from the Sun crosses about 1.5 × 10¹¹ m of nearly empty space to reach the Earth, a journey no sound could make, since sound needs air or some other material to carry it. In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell worked out a speed, 1/√(μ₀ε₀), from the laws of electricity and magnetism alone, and the number it gave, about 3 × 10⁸ m/s, was the measured speed of light.
That agreement told physicists what light is, and it means that a radio signal, the warmth from a fire and an X-ray are the same kind of wave as visible light, differing only in frequency.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what an electromagnetic wave is, place radio, light and X-rays on the spectrum and use c = fλ and t = d/c.
intro.whyItMatters: It ties the electrical half of the course to the wave half.

recap.keyIdea: Light is an electromagnetic wave travelling at c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum, and radio, light and X-rays differ only in frequency, with c = fλ.

blocks.text: Changing electric and magnetic fields sustain each other, so a disturbance travels through empty space at c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, and that wave is light. The same wave at a longer wavelength is a microwave or radio wave, and at a shorter one an X-ray, so one relation, c = fλ, links the frequency and wavelength of every band, and a distance divided by c gives the travel time.
The energy of a photon is hf, which grows with frequency.

recap.nextHook: The last part of the course turns to heat, and starts by separating heat from temperature.

lessons.title: Heat and temperature

reveal.text: The temperature rises by 5 K. The same energy is shared among twice as much water, so each kilogram gets half as much.

lead.text: The **temperature** of an object is a measure of the average energy of motion of its particles, and two objects in contact reach the same temperature when no energy passes between them, a state called thermal equilibrium. **Heat**, written Q, is something else: it is the energy that passes from one object to another because their temperatures differ. A hot object does not *contain* heat. It has [[internal energy|The total energy of motion and interaction of all the particles in an object.]], and heat is the name for the part of it that is transferred.

The heat Q needed to change the temperature of a mass m by ΔT is *Q = m c ΔT*, where c is the **specific heat**, the energy needed to warm 1 kg of the material by 1 K. It is in J/(kg K), and it differs from one material to another, as the figure shows.

afterFigure.text: Water has a high specific heat, 4186 J/(kg K), against 387 for copper. This is why the sea warms and cools slowly, with the result that coasts have milder weather than inland places: dry soil and rock have a specific heat of roughly 800 J/(kg K) and respond several times faster.

diagram.alt: A bar chart of specific heat in joules per kilogram kelvin: water 4186, ice 2090, aluminium 900 and copper 387. Water needs about eleven times as much energy as copper to warm by the same amount.
diagram.caption: Water needs far more energy per kilogram than a metal for the same temperature rise.

steps.headline: How much energy heats 2.0 kg of water by 30 K? Use c = 4186 J/(kg K).

workedSteps.text: Write the relation between the heat and the temperature change.
The mass, the specific heat and the temperature change all go into it.
That is about 251 kJ, which a 1 kW heater supplies in a little over four minutes.

steps.headline: A copper block of mass 0.50 kg is heated from 20 °C to 100 °C. Find the heat needed. The specific heat of copper is 387 J/(kg K).

workedSteps.text: Find the temperature change first.
The mass, the specific heat and this temperature change go into Q = m c ΔT.

reveal.text: The temperature stays at 0 °C while any ice is left: all the energy goes into melting it.

lead.text: Heat a kilogram of ice that starts at −20 °C, as in the figure, and the temperature rises until it reaches 0 °C. The temperature then stays at 0 °C while the ice melts, even though heat is still arriving, and it begins to rise again only when all the ice has become water. The same happens at 100 °C while the water boils. The energy in these flat stretches goes into freeing the particles from one another instead of making them move faster.

The energy needed per kilogram to change phase at a fixed temperature is the **latent heat**, and *Q = m L*. For melting ice the **latent heat of fusion** is L_f = 334 kJ/kg, and for boiling water the **latent heat of vaporisation** is L_v = 2260 kJ/kg.

afterFigure.text: The figure adds up the whole journey for 1 kg: 41.8 kJ to warm the ice from −20 °C to 0 °C (with c = 2090 J/(kg K) for ice), 334 kJ to melt it, 418.6 kJ to warm the water to 100 °C, and then 2260 kJ to boil it. Boiling takes about seven times the energy of melting, because the particles must be separated completely. It is why steam burns badly: condensing 1 kg of steam gives back the 2260 kJ.

diagram.alt: A heating curve for 1 kilogram of ice from minus 20 degrees Celsius. The temperature rises, stays at 0 degrees while 334 kilojoules melt the ice, rises again to 100 degrees, then stays at 100 degrees while 2260 kilojoules boil the water.
diagram.caption: Temperature against energy added. The flat parts are phase changes, where energy goes into changing the state and the temperature does not rise.

reveal.text: The energy melts the ice to water at 0 °C, and none of it raises the temperature.

lead.text: When a hot object and a cold one are put together in an insulated container, energy passes from the hot one to the cold one until both are at the same temperature, and none is lost. The energy lost by the hot object is therefore equal to the energy gained by the cold one: *m₁c₁(T₁ − T) = m₂c₂(T − T₂)*, where T is the final temperature. This method of finding the result is called **calorimetry**.

Take 1 kg of water at 80 °C and 2 kg at 20 °C. The same specific heat appears on both sides and cancels, so 1 × (80 − T) = 2 × (T − 20), which gives 80 − T = 2T − 40, so that 3T = 120 and T = 40 °C. The final temperature is nearer to 20 °C, because there is more cold water.

afterFigure.text: Where a change of phase occurs, its latent heat has to be added to the account. Energy is conserved throughout, so whatever the hot object gives up, in warming or melting or any other change, appears somewhere else in the same container.

steps.headline: Half a kilogram of water at 90 °C is mixed with 1.5 kg of water at 10 °C in an insulated container. Find the final temperature.

workedSteps.text: The specific heat of water is the same on both sides and cancels, so the energy balance is 0.50 × (90 − T) = 1.5 × (T − 10).
Expand both sides.
Gather the terms in T on one side and the numbers on the other, then solve for T.

reveal.text: The mixture settles at 25 °C, a quarter of the way from 10 °C up to 70 °C, since there is three times as much cold water.
The energy to melt the ice comes out of the warm water, and then the melted ice warms up from 0 °C to the final temperature as the water cools.

lessons.orientation: Calculate heat transfer with specific and latent heats.
lessons.nextAction: See how heat moves, by conduction through a material and by radiation across empty space.

blocks.text: Melting 1 kg of ice that is already at 0 °C takes 334 kJ, which is almost exactly the energy needed to warm the same kilogram of water from 0 °C to 80 °C. Water also takes eleven times as much energy as the same mass of copper to warm by one degree, so a kilogram of copper and a kilogram of water given equal amounts of energy end at very different temperatures.
Numbers like these show that the energy you put into a substance and the reading on a thermometer are different quantities, heat and temperature, linked through the mass and the material.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find the heat needed to warm or melt a substance and the final temperature when objects are mixed.
intro.whyItMatters: It lets you predict how long a kettle takes to boil, or how much ice cools a drink.

recap.keyIdea: Heat is energy in transit, Q = mcΔT while the temperature changes and Q = mL while the phase changes, and in a mixture the heat lost equals the heat gained.

blocks.text: Temperature measures the average energy of particles, and heat is the energy that moves because of a temperature difference. The heat to change a temperature is Q = mcΔT, and while a substance melts or boils the temperature stays fixed and the heat goes into the change of phase, Q = mL.
In an insulated mixture the energy lost by the hot parts equals the energy gained by the cold ones, which fixes the final temperature.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson follows the way heat moves, by conduction, convection and radiation.

lessons.title: How heat moves

reveal.text: The heat flow halves. The same temperature difference is spread over twice the thickness, which makes a weaker gradient to drive heat through.

lead.text: Heat can travel in three ways: by conduction through a material, by convection in a moving fluid, and by radiation across space. In **conduction**, energy passes from particle to particle without the material itself moving, always from the hotter side to the colder. There is no flow of cold: a cold window does not let cold in, it lets heat out. For a layer of area A and thickness L with a temperature difference ΔT between its faces, the rate of heat flow is *P = k A ΔT / L*, in watts.

The constant k is the **thermal conductivity** of the material, in W/(m K): about 400 for copper, 1.0 for glass, 0.50 for brick and 0.04 for a good insulator such as fibreglass. The rate grows with area and temperature difference and *falls with thickness*, so that doubling L halves it.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the same 20 K difference is spread across a brick wall 20 cm thick, which carries 50 W through each square metre, and across the same wall with 10 cm of insulation added. Each layer takes a share of the temperature drop in proportion to L/k, and almost all of the drop falls across the insulation. For layers in series the rates combine as *P = A ΔT / (L₁/k₁ + L₂/k₂)*, which gives 6.9 W per square metre for the second wall.

diagram.alt: Cross-sections of a wall with a temperature graph beneath. A single brick layer 20 cm thick has its temperature fall steadily from 20 degrees inside to 0 outside. With 10 cm of insulation added, most of the temperature drop happens across the insulation and the heat flow is far smaller.
diagram.caption: The temperature falls across each layer in proportion to the thickness divided by the conductivity. Use the buttons to compare one layer and two.

steps.headline: A glass pane of 3.0 m² and thickness 6.0 mm has 15 K across it. Find the heat conducted, with k = 1.0 W/(m K).

workedSteps.text: Write the rate formula.
Convert the thickness to metres, 6.0 mm = 0.0060 m, and substitute.
The substituted expression gives the rate of heat flow.
That is 7.5 kW, as much as several electric fires, which is why single glazing loses so much heat.

steps.headline: A brick wall of area 12 m² and thickness 0.20 m has k = 0.50 W/(m K), and the temperature difference across it is 15 K. Find the heat flow through it.

workedSteps.text: Write the formula.
Substitute the values into the formula.

lead.text: **Convection** is heat carried by the bulk motion of a fluid. Air heated by a radiator expands, becomes less dense and rises, and cooler air moves in to take its place, so that the room circulates. **Radiation** is different in kind: a hot surface emits electromagnetic waves, the infrared met in 'Light as an electromagnetic wave', which cross a vacuum and warm whatever absorbs them. It is how the Sun warms the Earth, through 150 million kilometres of nothing.

afterFigure.text: Every object above absolute zero radiates, not only hot ones. You emit infrared now, and the walls of the room emit it back at you, and what matters for the warmth you feel is the *difference* between the two.

reveal.text: The radiated power rises by a factor of 81, because it depends on the fourth power of the kelvin temperature, and 3⁴ = 81.

lead.text: The kelvin temperature is the Celsius temperature plus 273.15, so that 0 K is absolute zero and 300 K is about 27 °C. A surface of area A at temperature T radiates the power *P = ε σ A T⁴*, where σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/(m² K⁴) is the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and ε is the **emissivity**, a number between 0 and 1 that describes how well the surface radiates. A dull black surface has ε close to 1, and a polished silver one close to 0.
A black surface at 300 K radiates 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × 300⁴ = 459 W for every square metre. At 600 K, twice the temperature, it radiates 7348 W/m², **16 times as much**, as the graph shows.

afterFigure.text: The same emissivity governs absorption, so a good radiator is also a good absorber, and a surface exchanges energy with its surroundings in both directions. The net power is *P = ε σ A (T⁴ − T_surroundings⁴)*, which is why a vacuum flask has silvered walls: a low emissivity cuts radiation, the vacuum between the walls removes conduction and convection, and the contents stay hot.

diagram.alt: A graph of radiated power per square metre against temperature in kelvin for a black surface. It rises from 0 at 0 K to 459 watts per square metre at 300 K and 7348 at 600 K, which is 16 times as much.
diagram.caption: Radiated power rises with the fourth power of the kelvin temperature. Doubling the temperature from 300 K to 600 K multiplies it by 16.

steps.headline: A person has a skin area of 1.5 m² and skin temperature 33 °C, in a room at 20 °C. Take the emissivity as 0.97. Find the net power radiated.

workedSteps.text: Convert both temperatures to kelvin.
Write the net power.
Substitute. The two fourth powers are 306⁴ = 8.77 × 10⁹ and 293⁴ = 7.37 × 10⁹.
The expression gives the net power radiated.
That is about 115 W, close to the rate at which the body produces heat at rest.

reveal.text: The power is 2613 W. A shiny surface with ε = 0.05 would radiate only a small fraction of that.
The wall now loses 121 W instead of 500 W, though the insulation adds only a quarter to its thickness, because the insulation has a far smaller conductivity.

lessons.orientation: Compute conduction rates and radiated power, and see why insulation and colour matter.
lessons.nextAction: Count the energy of a gas, and use the ideal gas law and the first law of thermodynamics.

blocks.text: A single glass pane 5 mm thick and 2 m² in area, with the inside at 20 K higher than the outside, carries 8000 W of heat through it, as much as several electric fires. Fix a 10 cm layer of insulation to the wall in place of the glass and the same temperature difference drives only about 16 W. Heat leaves a warm object in three ways, and conduction through a layer of material is the easiest of them to calculate.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to calculate heat flow through a layer, find radiated power from the fourth-power law and say what insulation and surface colour do.
intro.whyItMatters: It is how a house, a flask or a spacecraft is designed to hold its heat.

recap.keyIdea: Conduction gives a heat flow P = kAΔT/L, which halves when the thickness doubles, and radiation gives P = εσAT⁴, which multiplies by 16 when the kelvin temperature doubles.

blocks.text: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation. The conduction rate through a layer is kAΔT/L, so a thicker or lower-conductivity layer slows it, and layers in series add their L/k. A surface radiates εσAT⁴ at kelvin temperature T, so a small rise in temperature makes a large rise in power, and the net exchange depends on the difference of T⁴ between the object and its surroundings.
Heat flows from hot to cold, and there is no flow of cold.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson looks at the energy of a gas, and at how heat and work together change it.

lessons.title: Gases and the first law

reveal.text: The pressure doubles, because it is proportional to the kelvin temperature at fixed volume. The next screen gives the equation behind this.

lead.text: A gas is a very large number of molecules moving at random, and the **pressure** on a wall is the average force per unit area from all their collisions with it. The kelvin temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules. Raising it makes the molecules faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often, and in the figure the pressure doubles when the temperature does.

For a gas at low density, called an **ideal gas**, these relations combine into one equation, the **ideal gas law**: *P V = n R T*. Here P is the pressure in pascals, V the volume in cubic metres, n the amount of gas in moles, T the temperature in **kelvin**, and R = 8.314 J/(mol K) is the gas constant.

afterFigure.text: The temperature must be in kelvin, because the equation says that P is proportional to T and the Celsius zero is not a true zero. Using 27 °C in place of 300 K makes the pressure come out wrong by a factor of more than ten. For 2.0 mol at 300 K in a volume of 0.050 m³ the pressure is 2.0 × 8.314 × 300 / 0.050 = 99 768 Pa, or 99.8 kPa.

diagram.alt: A rigid box containing twelve gas molecules with arrows showing their velocities. At 300 K the arrows are short and the pressure is 99.8 kPa. At 600 K the arrows are longer, the molecules move faster, and the pressure is 199.5 kPa.
diagram.caption: The same box and the same gas at two temperatures. Faster molecules hit the walls harder and more often.

steps.headline: Find the pressure of 1.5 mol of an ideal gas at 290 K in a volume of 0.030 m³.

workedSteps.text: Rearrange PV = nRT for the pressure.
The temperature is already in kelvin, so the values go straight into the formula.
That is a little above atmospheric pressure at sea level, which is about 101 kPa.

steps.headline: Find the volume of 1.0 mol of an ideal gas at 300 K and a pressure of 100 kPa, which is 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa.

workedSteps.text: Rearrange PV = nRT for the volume.
Substitute the values.
The volume comes out in cubic metres, and 1 m³ = 1000 L.

lead.text: A gas that expands pushes on its surroundings, and so does work on them. If the pressure stays constant while the volume increases by ΔV, the work done by the gas is *W = P ΔV*. A gas at 100 kPa that expands from 0.010 m³ to 0.030 m³ does W = 1.0 × 10⁵ × 0.020 = 2000 J. On a graph of pressure against volume, called a **PV diagram**, this is the area of the shaded rectangle under the path.

When the pressure changes during the expansion the work is still the area under the path, whatever its shape. If the same gas expands between the same volumes while its temperature is held constant, the pressure falls as the volume grows, the area is smaller, and the work is 1099 J. When the volume does not change, there is no area and no work.

afterFigure.text: The work depends on the path and not just on the two end points, which is why the figure gives a different answer for each path. Work done *by* the gas is positive, and work done *on* the gas, when it is compressed, counts as negative.

diagram.alt: Three pressure-volume graphs. A gas expanding at 100 kPa from 0.010 to 0.030 cubic metres does 2000 joules of work, the area of the shaded rectangle. Expanding at constant temperature between the same volumes it does 1099 joules, the area under a curve. At constant volume there is no area and no work.
diagram.caption: The work done by an expanding gas is the area under its pressure-volume graph. Use the buttons to compare three paths.

lead.text: The **first law of thermodynamics** is the conservation of energy applied to heat and work: *ΔU = Q − W*. Here ΔU is the change in the internal energy of the gas, Q the heat added to it, and W the work done *by* the gas on its surroundings. Heat added raises the internal energy, and work done by the gas takes it away, so a gas that absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work gains 500 − 200 = 300 J of internal energy.

For an ideal gas the internal energy depends only on the temperature. This is why adding heat does not always raise the temperature: a gas that expands as it is heated does work, and some of the energy leaves as work.

afterFigure.text: Three special cases follow from the law. At constant temperature, ΔU = 0, so Q = W and all the heat added becomes work. At constant volume, W = 0, so ΔU = Q and all the heat raises the energy. At constant pressure the heat both raises the energy and pays for the work of expansion P ΔV.

steps.headline: A gas absorbs 800 J of heat and does 350 J of work on its surroundings. Find the change in its internal energy.

workedSteps.text: Write the first law.
The gas absorbs heat, so Q is positive, and it does work on its surroundings, so W is positive. Substituting gives the change in internal energy.
The internal energy rises, so the temperature of the gas rises too.

reveal.text: Work done *on* the gas counts as a negative W, and heat leaving counts as a negative Q.
Only the part of the heat that is not spent on the expansion raises the internal energy.

lessons.orientation: Use the ideal gas law and the first law of thermodynamics.
lessons.nextAction: Ask how much of the heat in an engine can be turned into work, and find the limit.

blocks.text: A gas sealed in a box presses on every wall, and the push comes from an enormous number of molecules striking the walls and bouncing off, each collision adding a tiny force. Heat a gas in a cylinder closed by a movable piston and it does something more, since it expands and pushes the piston, and whatever rests on it, outwards, so that part of the energy supplied leaves the gas as work and does not warm it.

Two short equations describe all of this: the **ideal gas law**, which connects the pressure, volume, amount and temperature of a gas, and the **first law of thermodynamics**, which keeps account of the energy by sharing the heat supplied between the work the gas does and the rise in its internal energy.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to use PV = nRT with kelvin temperatures, find the work done by a gas from a PV diagram and apply the first law.
intro.whyItMatters: Every engine and refrigerator is a gas passing through these steps.

recap.keyIdea: An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT with T in kelvin, it does work PΔV when it expands, and the first law says ΔU = Q − W.

blocks.text: Gas pressure comes from molecular collisions, and for an ideal gas it obeys PV = nRT with the temperature in kelvin. A gas that expands does work equal to the area under its PV diagram, which is PΔV at constant pressure, and the first law, ΔU = Q − W, accounts for where the heat added goes.
At constant temperature the heat equals the work, and at constant volume the heat equals the change in internal energy.

recap.nextHook: The last lesson asks how much of the heat taken in by an engine can become work, and why entropy limits it.

lessons.title: Engines and the limit

reveal.text: Even such a perfect engine must reject some heat. No cycle of this kind can turn all of the heat from one reservoir into work, which is the second law of thermodynamics, and the next screen shows the heat that every engine passes on to something colder.

lead.text: A petrol engine, a steam turbine and a jet engine all work in the same way. They take heat Q_h from something hot, such as burning fuel or steam, turn part of it into work W, and reject the remainder Q_c to something colder, such as the air or a river. By the [[first law|Energy is conserved: ΔU = Q − W. Met in 'Gases and the first law'.]], applied to an engine that returns to its starting state after each cycle, *W = Q_h − Q_c*.

The **efficiency** of the engine is the fraction of the heat taken in that becomes work, *e = W / Q_h*. In the figure a real engine takes in 1000 J, rejects 700 J and so produces 300 J of work, which gives e = 300 / 1000 = 0.30.

afterFigure.text: The hot and cold places are called **reservoirs**, bodies large enough that taking heat from them or giving heat to them does not change their temperature. The heat rejected to the cold reservoir is not a loss through bad design.

diagram.alt: An engine between a hot reservoir and a cold reservoir with arrows whose widths show the energy in joules. A real engine takes 1000 joules, produces 300 of work and rejects 700. An ideal engine between 600 and 300 kelvin produces 500 joules of work and rejects 500. A perfect engine that rejects nothing is not possible.
diagram.caption: Heat in, work out and heat rejected, with arrow width showing the energy. Use the buttons to compare three engines.

reveal.text: The work done in each cycle is 1200 − 900 = 300 J, and the efficiency is the work divided by the heat taken in, which is 0.25.

lead.text: In 1824 Sadi Carnot analysed the best that any engine could do between a hot reservoir at temperature T_h and a cold reservoir at T_c. No engine working between those two temperatures can be more efficient than *e = 1 − T_c / T_h*, with both temperatures in kelvin. An engine that reaches this value is called a **Carnot engine**, and no real engine does.
Between 600 K and 300 K the limit is 1 − 300/600 = 0.50. This is the second case in the first figure, where 1000 J gives 500 J of work and 500 J is rejected.

afterFigure.text: The limit explains the design of power stations: steam is made as hot as the materials allow, and the exhaust is cooled by a river or the air. It also shows that **efficiency does not depend on the engine's design alone**, since even a perfect engine is limited by its two temperatures, and that the limit reaches 1 only if T_c were absolute zero.

Marked points: 0.50 for 600 and 300 kelvin and 0.60 for 700 and 280 kelvin.
diagram.caption: The lower the ratio of the cold to the hot temperature, the higher the limit. Every real engine lies below this line.

steps.headline: Find the greatest possible efficiency of an engine working between 800 K and 360 K.

workedSteps.text: Write the Carnot limit.
Both temperatures are already in kelvin. Substitute.
The ratio of the two temperatures is taken away from 1.
A real engine between these temperatures would do worse than this.

steps.headline: Find the greatest possible efficiency of an engine working between 750 K and 225 K.

workedSteps.text: Write the Carnot limit.
Both temperatures are in kelvin, so they go straight into the limit.

lead.text: Why must heat be rejected? The answer is a quantity called **entropy**, S. When heat Q enters an object at a steady temperature T, its entropy changes by *ΔS = Q / T*, in J/K. Melting 1.0 kg of ice at 273.15 K takes 334 000 J, so the entropy of the ice rises by 334 000 / 273.15 = 1223 J/K. The same heat adds more entropy at a low temperature than at a high one.

The **second law of thermodynamics** says that the total entropy of an isolated system and everything it exchanges heat with never decreases. Suppose 1000 J flows from a hot object at 400 K to a cold one at 300 K. The hot one loses 1000 / 400 = 2.5 J/K and the cold one gains 1000 / 300 = 3.33 J/K, so the total rises by 0.83 J/K.

afterFigure.text: The reverse flow, from cold to hot with nothing else changing, would lower the total entropy by 0.83 J/K, and it never happens. This is the reason an engine must reject heat: the 1000 J taken from a reservoir at T_h removes Q/T_h of entropy, and some heat must pass to the cold reservoir to add at least as much. Entropy is often called disorder, but it is better described as a count of the number of ways in which the energy can be spread out, which rises when heat flows from hot to cold.

reveal.text: The entropy rises by 489 J/K. The molecules in liquid water can be arranged in many more ways than those in an ice crystal.

steps.headline: Heat of 600 J flows from an object at 500 K to one at 300 K. Find the total change in entropy.

workedSteps.text: The hot object loses entropy and the cold one gains it. The hot object changes by −Q/T_h.
The cold object gains the same heat at its own temperature, so its entropy changes by Q/T_c.
Adding the two changes gives the total.

lead.text: Run an engine in reverse and work goes in, heat is taken from the cold reservoir, and a larger amount of heat is delivered to the hot one. This is a **heat pump**, or a refrigerator when the cold side is what matters. The work is needed because heat does not flow from cold to hot by itself, as the entropy argument showed.

The measure of a heat pump is the ratio of the heat delivered to the work used, the **coefficient of performance**, and the best possible value is *T_h / (T_h − T_c)*. A pump heating a house at 293 K from outdoor air at 273 K could in the ideal case deliver 293 / 20 = 14.65 J of heat for each joule of work.

afterFigure.text: Real machines come nowhere near that figure, though a good heat pump delivers several times as much heat as the electrical energy it uses, which is why it beats a plain electric heater, whose ratio is exactly 1. The closer the two temperatures, the less work is needed per joule moved.

reveal.text: The ideal ratio is 10.93, so each joule of work delivers 10.93 J of heat to the house, which no real pump achieves.
The Carnot limit for these temperatures is 0.625, and the station reaches 0.40, which is typical of a real plant.

lessons.orientation: Find the efficiency limit of a heat engine and compute entropy changes.
lessons.nextAction: You can now calculate waves, fields, induction, heat and the limits on engines, using one equation for each.

blocks.text: A power station that raises steam at 800 K and cools it with river water at 300 K turns only part of the heat from its fuel into electricity, and the rest flows into the river.
How large a part can become work is settled by the **second law of thermodynamics**, and the answer depends on the two temperatures between which the engine works.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to find an engine's efficiency, state the Carnot limit and calculate the entropy change when heat enters at a fixed temperature.
intro.whyItMatters: It explains why every engine, power station and refrigerator is limited by two temperatures.

recap.keyIdea: No engine can exceed e = 1 − T_c/T_h in kelvin, and when heat Q enters at temperature T the entropy changes by Q/T, with the total never falling.

blocks.text: An engine turns heat Q_h into work W and rejects Q_c, with efficiency W/Q_h and a limit of 1 − T_c/T_h set by the two kelvin temperatures. The second law explains the limit: heat Q entering at temperature T changes entropy by Q/T, and a cycle that took heat from one reservoir and turned it all into work would lower the total entropy.
Run backwards, the same machine becomes a refrigerator or heat pump, which uses work to move heat from cold to hot.

questions.prompt: A pendulum takes 0.25 s to swing out and back to where it started, which is one complete cycle. What is its frequency, in hertz?
hints: Frequency counts the cycles in one second.
How many times does 0.25 s go into 1 s?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period: f = 1 / 0.25 s = 4 Hz.

questions.onCorrect: Four cycles fit into each second, so the pendulum has a frequency of 4 Hz. Period and frequency are reciprocals.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the period itself. Frequency is its reciprocal, the number of cycles per second.
Divide 1 s by 0.25 s to count the cycles in a second.

questions.prompt: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring, pulled 4 cm from rest and released, has a period of 0.314 s. If the same mass is pulled only 2 cm and released, how does the period compare with 0.314 s?
hints: The amplitude and the period are different quantities.
Compare how far the mass travels with how hard the spring pulls.

acceptedIdeas: The same, because the weaker pull and shorter distance cancel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same, because the weaker pull and shorter distance cancel

questions.onCorrect: For a spring the period does not depend on the amplitude: half the distance is covered at half the acceleration.

misconceptions.feedback: Less distance is covered, but the pull is also weaker, so the mass moves more slowly. Both changes matter, and they have to be weighed against each other.
A weaker pull does slow the mass, but it also has less distance to cover. Both changes matter, and they have to be weighed against each other.

choices.label: Shorter, because the mass has less distance to cover each cycle
The same, because the weaker pull and shorter distance cancel
Longer, because a smaller stretch gives a weaker push on the mass

questions.prompt: What is the square root of 0.0025, in seconds?
hints: Find a number that multiplied by itself gives 0.0025.
questions.onCorrect: The root of 0.0025 s² is 0.05 s, and this one square root is the only awkward step in the formula.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the value before the root. Find the number that multiplies by itself to give 0.0025.
0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. Check the decimal places.

questions.prompt: A 2.0 kg mass hangs on a spring with k = 50 N/m, so that T = 2π × 0.2 s. What is the period, in seconds to three decimal places?
questions.onCorrect: The period is 1.257 s, a little over one second, since this mass is heavy and the spring is soft.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the square root before the factor 2π is applied.
That is m/k. Take its root, then multiply by 2π.

questions.prompt: Two pendulums are each 1 m long. One carries a 0.1 kg bob and the other a 1.0 kg bob, and both are swung through a few degrees. How does the period of the 1.0 kg bob compare with that of the 0.1 kg bob?
hints: Compare the pull of gravity with the mass being accelerated.
Look for a quantity that appears on both the top and bottom of a ratio.

acceptedIdeas: The same, because the pull and the mass to move both grow tenfold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same, because the pull and the mass to move both grow tenfold

questions.onCorrect: The mass cancels, so a pendulum's period depends only on its length and on g.

misconceptions.feedback: The heavy bob is harder to accelerate, but gravity also pulls on it ten times harder. Both changes matter, and they have to be weighed against each other.
Gravity does pull harder on the heavy bob, but there is also more mass to accelerate. Both changes matter, and they have to be weighed against each other.

choices.label: Longer, because the heavy bob is ten times harder to accelerate
The same, because the pull and the mass to move both grow tenfold
Shorter, because gravity pulls on the heavy bob ten times harder

questions.prompt: A pendulum has a period of 2 s, and a second pendulum in the same room is nine times as long. What is the period of the longer pendulum, in seconds?
hints: Which quantity in T = 2π√(L/g) changes, and which stay the same?
If L becomes 9L, what happens to √L?
Multiply the original period by that factor.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T is proportional to √L, and √9 = 3, so the period triples: 2 s × 3 = 6 s.

questions.onCorrect: The period triples, since √9 = 3. To triple a pendulum's period you must make it nine times as long.

misconceptions.feedback: That scales T in step with L. The period depends on the square root of the length.
That squares the factor. Period depends on √L, so a factor of 9 in length gives 3 in period.

questions.prompt: A pendulum 1 m long is carried to the Moon, where g is 1.62 m/s² instead of 9.8 m/s², with its length and its bob unchanged. What is its period on the Moon, in seconds, to two decimal places?
hints: Only g changes in the formula.
Take the square root and multiply by 2π.
questions.onCorrect: The weaker pull makes the restoring force smaller, so the swing is slower, 4.94 s against 2.01 s on Earth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the period on Earth. The Moon's weaker gravity changes g.
That divides by too much. Use L/g = 1/1.62 under the root.

questions.prompt: A 0.20 kg mass hangs on a spring with k = 20 N/m. What is its period, in seconds?
hints: The root of 0.01 is 0.1; now multiply by 2π.
questions.onCorrect: The period is 0.628 s. Mass and stiffness are the only quantities in the formula.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the square root alone. Multiply by 2π.
That is m/k. Take the square root, then multiply by 2π.

questions.prompt: A pendulum is 0.25 m long. Using g = 9.8 m/s², what is its period, in seconds?
hints: Take the root, about 0.16, and multiply by 2π.
questions.onCorrect: A 0.25 m pendulum takes about one second, a quarter of the length of the 1 m pendulum and half its period.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2π × 0.25. The length goes under a square root, and g divides it.
That is the period of a 1 m pendulum.

questions.prompt: A mass on a spring oscillates at 2.5 Hz. The mass is replaced by one four times as large on the same spring. What is the new frequency, in hertz?
hints: Four times the mass changes the period by what factor?
Frequency is the reciprocal of the period.
If the period doubles, the frequency halves.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T scales as √m, so four times the mass doubles T, which halves f: 2.5 / 2 = 1.25 Hz.

questions.onCorrect: Quadrupling the mass doubles the period and so halves the frequency, from 2.5 Hz to 1.25 Hz.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 4. The period depends on √m, so the factor is 2.
That multiplies by 4. A larger mass makes the oscillation slower.

questions.prompt: A cork floats on a lake, and a train of wave crests moves steadily from left to right across the water, passing the cork one after another. After several crests have passed, where is the cork?
hints: Think about what moves along the lake and what only moves up and down.
Watch a single piece of the water rather than the crests.

acceptedIdeas: Close to where it started, having moved up and down
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Close to where it started, having moved up and down

questions.onCorrect: The pattern moves across the lake, but each piece of water only moves in a small path about its starting point.

misconceptions.feedback: The wave moves across the water, but the water does not travel with it, so the cork is not carried along.
Nothing in the wave pushes the cork under. It rises and falls with the surface.

choices.label: Carried a long way to the right with the waves
Sunk below the surface
Close to where it started, having moved up and down

questions.prompt: What is 343 divided by 440, in metres, to two decimal places?
questions.onCorrect: A 440 Hz note in air has a wavelength of 0.78 m, which is a useful size to remember for concert pitch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 440 / 343. The speed goes on top: λ = v / f.
That multiplies instead of dividing. λ = v / f.

questions.prompt: A radio station broadcasts at 100 MHz, which is 100 × 10⁶ Hz, and radio waves travel at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the wavelength of the station's radio wave, in metres?
hints: Divide the speed by the frequency.
questions.onCorrect: The wavelength is 3.0 m. Radio waves have long wavelengths because their frequencies are low compared with their speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the frequency by the speed. Use λ = v / f.
That leaves the frequency in MHz. Convert 100 MHz to 1.00 × 10⁸ Hz first.

questions.prompt: A 440 Hz note travels through air at 20 °C at 343 m/s. A violinist then plays an 880 Hz note, one octave higher, in the same air. How fast does the 880 Hz note travel?
hints: The medium sets the speed of sound.
Does the air change when the pitch changes?

acceptedIdeas: About 343 m/s, the same as the 440 Hz note
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 343 m/s, the same as the 440 Hz note

questions.onCorrect: In a given medium the speed is fixed. Doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher note has a shorter wavelength, not a lower speed. Ask what sets the speed of sound, and whether the air changes with the pitch.
The speed of sound is set by the air rather than by the note. Ask whether doubling the frequency changes the air.

choices.label: About 171 m/s, half as fast as the 440 Hz note
About 343 m/s, the same as the 440 Hz note
About 686 m/s, twice as fast as the 440 Hz note

questions.prompt: Ultrasound scanners send sound waves, too high-pitched to hear, through the soft tissue of the body. As an ultrasound wave passes, the particles of the tissue move
hints: Is ultrasound a different kind of wave from the sound you hear?
Which direction does a compression travel in?

acceptedIdeas: Back and forth along the direction of travel
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Back and forth along the direction of travel

questions.onCorrect: Ultrasound is sound at a frequency above hearing, so like sound in air it is longitudinal, and the particles oscillate along the direction the compression travels.

misconceptions.feedback: That describes a transverse wave, and ultrasound is sound, which is longitudinal.
The pattern travels on through the tissue, but the particles only shuffle about their positions.
The particles move back and forth along a line, not in circles.

choices.label: Back and forth along the direction of travel
Along with the wave to the listener
Up and down across the direction of travel
In circles

questions.prompt: A 660 Hz sound wave in air, 0.52 m long, passes into a swimming pool, where sound travels at about 1480 m/s. What is the wavelength of the sound in the water, in metres?
hints: Which quantity is the same on both sides of the boundary?
Use the new speed with the same frequency.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The frequency is unchanged: λ = v / f = 1480 / 660 = 2.24 m.

questions.onCorrect: The wavelength grows from 0.52 m to 2.24 m because the speed rises while the frequency stays at 660 Hz.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wavelength in air. The speed changes in water, and the frequency does not.
That divides the frequency by the speed. Use λ = v / f with v = 1480 m/s.
That is the wavelength of a 440 Hz note in water. This note is 660 Hz.

questions.prompt: Green light has a frequency of 6.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz and travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a vacuum. What is its wavelength, in nanometres? (1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m)
hints: The result is in metres: 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ m.
A nanometre is 10⁻⁹ m, so multiply by 10⁹.
questions.onCorrect: Visible light has wavelengths of a few hundred nanometres, much shorter than the 3 m of a radio wave.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the wavelength in metres. The question asks for nanometres.
That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.prompt: A wave on a rope has a frequency of 8 Hz and a wavelength of 0.50 m. What is its speed, in metres per second?
hints: Multiply the frequency by the wavelength.
Eight cycles each second, 0.50 m of pattern per cycle.
questions.onCorrect: The pattern advances 0.50 m for each of 8 cycles in a second, so it moves at 4 m/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the frequency by the wavelength. Multiply them.
That divides the wavelength by the frequency.

questions.prompt: What is the name for a wave in which the medium moves along the direction of travel? Give one word.
hints: Sound in air is an example.
The other kind is called transverse.
questions.onCorrect: Longitudinal waves such as sound have the medium moving along the line of travel, in compressions and spreads.

misconceptions.feedback: A transverse wave has the medium moving across the direction of travel, like a rope.

questions.prompt: Two pulses travel along a rope in opposite directions, one 3 cm high and one 2 cm high, both on the same side of the rope. At the moment their centres coincide, how high is the rope at that point?
hints: Do the pulses push on each other, or does each one displace the rope separately?
Both pulses lift the rope on the same side.
questions.onCorrect: Where waves overlap, their displacements add. Afterwards each pulse continues as though the other were absent.

misconceptions.feedback: The smaller pulse does not disappear where it meets the larger one. Both lift the rope at the same moment, so their heights add to 5 cm.
Each pulse lifts the rope by its own height at the same time, so the two lifts add, giving 5 cm, and are not shared out.
Waves pass through each other without colliding the way balls do, and while they overlap the rope rises to the sum of their heights, 5 cm.

choices.label: 0 cm, because the pulses collide and stop
About 2.5 cm, the average of the two heights
5 cm, the two heights added
3 cm, the height of the taller pulse

questions.prompt: Two waves on a rope each have an amplitude of 2.5 cm, and they arrive at one point so that a crest of one meets a trough of the other. What is the displacement of the rope at that point, in centimetres?
hints: Add the two displacements, keeping their signs.
A trough is a displacement in the opposite direction.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The crest gives +2.5 cm and the trough −2.5 cm, and the sum is 0 cm.

questions.onCorrect: The two waves cancel completely at that point, though both are still travelling and pass on afterwards.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes, as if both were crests. A trough has the opposite sign.
That counts one wave only. Both displace the rope.

questions.prompt: What is the frequency of the third harmonic of this string, in hertz?
questions.onCorrect: The third harmonic is three times the fundamental. The harmonics of a string are whole-number multiples of its lowest frequency.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fundamental, n = 1.
That is the second harmonic, n = 2.

questions.prompt: What is the frequency of the fifth harmonic, in hertz?
questions.onCorrect: The fifth harmonic is 625 Hz. A longer string has a lower fundamental for the same wave speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fundamental.
That is the second harmonic.

questions.prompt: Two tuning forks, one at 440 Hz and one at 444 Hz, are struck together. How often does the sound swell to its loudest?
hints: The pattern depends on how far apart the two frequencies are.
Compare the number of cycles each fork makes in one second.

acceptedIdeas: About 4 times a second, as one fork gains 4 cycles each second
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 4 times a second, as one fork gains 4 cycles each second

questions.onCorrect: The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies, here 4 per second.

misconceptions.feedback: Two forks at slightly different frequencies drift in and out of step, so the sum does not stay steady. Ask how often they drift all the way round.
The pitch you hear is close to the average, 442 Hz, but the swells in loudness come far more slowly than that. Ask how quickly one fork gains on the other.

choices.label: About 442 times a second, since that is the average frequency
About 4 times a second, as one fork gains 4 cycles each second
Never, since the loudness stays steady while both forks sound

questions.prompt: Light of 450 nm passes through two slits 0.12 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away. What is the spacing between neighbouring bright fringes, in centimetres?
hints: Use y = λL/d, with every length in metres.
0.12 mm is 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ m and 450 nm is 4.5 × 10⁻⁷ m.
questions.onCorrect: The answer in metres is 0.0075 m. Converting every length to metres first avoids a slip of powers of ten.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer in metres. The question asks for centimetres.
That has the wavelength and the separation the wrong way up.

questions.prompt: A guitar string carries waves at 200 m/s, and a guitarist presses it against a fret so that its vibrating length is only 0.40 m. What is the fundamental frequency of the shortened string, in hertz?
questions.onCorrect: Shortening the string from 0.5 m to 0.4 m raises the fundamental from 200 Hz to 250 Hz.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fundamental for 0.5 m. Use L = 0.40 m.
That leaves out the factor 2 in 2L.

questions.prompt: A string 0.60 m long carries waves at 180 m/s. What is the frequency of its third harmonic, in hertz?
hints: 2L = 1.2 m, so the fundamental is 180 / 1.2 = 150 Hz.
questions.onCorrect: The fundamental is 150 Hz and the third harmonic is 450 Hz, three times as high.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fundamental.
That leaves out the factor 2 in 2L.

questions.prompt: Two sources sound at 220 Hz and 223 Hz together. How many loud swells are heard in 10 seconds?
hints: Multiply the rate by the time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The beat frequency is 223 − 220 = 3 per second, so 10 s contains 30 beats.

questions.onCorrect: A beat frequency of 3 per second gives 30 swells in 10 seconds.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the rate per second. The question asks about 10 seconds.
That adds the frequencies and multiplies by the time. The beat rate is their difference.

questions.prompt: Light of 600 nm passes slits 0.30 mm apart onto a screen 1.5 m away. What is the spacing of the bright fringes, in millimetres?
hints: Use y = λL/d with all lengths in metres.
questions.onCorrect: The fringes are 3.0 mm apart, a small spacing because the slits are wider apart than in the earlier example.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the answer in centimetres. The question asks for millimetres.
That leaves the answer in micrometres.

questions.prompt: What is log₁₀ of 1 000 000 000?
hints: The logarithm is the power of 10 that gives the number.
Write the billion as a power of 10.
questions.onCorrect: The logarithm of 10 raised to a power is just that power, so 10 log₁₀(10⁹) = 90.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the 10 in front of the log, not the value of the log.
That is the number itself. The logarithm is the power of 10 that gives it.

questions.prompt: One machine in a workshop gives a sound level of 70 dB where you stand. If ten identical machines run together at the same distance, roughly what is the total level?
hints: Intensities add when sources run together, but levels do not.
A level in decibels counts powers of ten in intensity.

acceptedIdeas: About 80 dB, ten more than one machine
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 80 dB, ten more than one machine

questions.onCorrect: Intensities add, but the level of the sum rises only by 10 log₁₀ of the factor.

misconceptions.feedback: Ten machines give ten times the intensity, but decibels count powers of ten in intensity, so the level does not rise tenfold.
Each machine adds its own intensity, so ten of them give ten times the intensity of one, and that has to raise the level.

choices.label: About 700 dB, ten times the level of one
About 80 dB, ten more than one machine
About 70 dB, the same as one machine

questions.prompt: One machine in a workshop gives 70 dB on its own, and two more identical machines are switched on beside it. By how many decibels does the level rise, to one decimal place?
hints: Three machines give three times the intensity of one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The intensity triples, so ΔL = 10 log₁₀ 3 = 4.77 dB, or 4.8 dB.

questions.onCorrect: Tripling the intensity is always about +4.8 dB, whatever the starting level, so three machines give about 74.8 dB.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the level of one machine. The question asks for the rise.
That triples the decibels. Tripling the intensity changes the level by a much smaller step.
That is the step for a doubling. Three machines give three times the intensity, so use log₁₀ 3.
That is the step for four machines, two doublings. Three machines give three times the intensity.

questions.prompt: An ambulance with its siren sounding at a steady 500 Hz drives straight towards you. What do you hear while the ambulance is approaching?
hints: Think about where the wave fronts end up as the source moves into its own waves.
Compare the wavelength ahead of the source with the wavelength at rest.
questions.onCorrect: A source moving towards you shortens the wavelength reaching you, and the same wave speed gives a higher frequency.

misconceptions.feedback: The wave fronts are squeezed together ahead of the source, which raises the frequency heard.
The siren does sound at 500 Hz, but the motion of the source changes what a listener receives.

choices.label: A frequency lower than 500 Hz
Exactly 500 Hz, until the ambulance passes
A frequency higher than 500 Hz

questions.prompt: What frequency does the listener hear, to the nearest hertz?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f' = 600 × 343 / 308.7 = 666.7 Hz, or 667 Hz to the nearest hertz.

questions.onCorrect: The listener hears 667 Hz, which is 11% above the true 600 Hz for a source moving at a tenth of the speed of sound.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the frequency of the source. The listener's frequency is raised by the approach.
That is the frequency for a receding source. For an approaching source use v − vₛ.

questions.prompt: What frequency does the listener hear, to the nearest hertz?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f' = 600 × 343 / 377.3 = 545.5 Hz, or 545 Hz to the nearest hertz.

questions.onCorrect: The frequency falls to 545 Hz after the siren has passed, and the drop of 122 Hz is larger than the rise of 67 Hz on the way in.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the frequency while it approaches. A receding source stretches the waves.
That is the frequency of the source. Motion changes the frequency received.

questions.prompt: A 450 Hz speaker stands at rest beside a track, and you ride towards it on a train at 60 m/s, with sound travelling at 343 m/s in the air. What frequency do you hear, to the nearest hertz?
hints: The source is at rest, so use the moving-listener formula.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: f' = f (v + v_o)/v = 450 × 403 / 343 = 528.7 Hz, or 529 Hz to the nearest hertz.

questions.onCorrect: A moving listener hears 529 Hz, compared with 545 Hz if the speaker moved towards you at the same speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the result for a moving source. The listener formula is f (v + v_o)/v.
The listener's motion does change the received frequency.

questions.prompt: An ambulance with an 800 Hz siren moves at 25 m/s towards a person standing on the pavement, with sound travelling at 343 m/s. What frequency does the person hear, to the nearest hertz?
hints: Is it the source or the listener that moves?
questions.onCorrect: The siren is heard at 863 Hz, about a semitone above its true pitch.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the frequency emitted. The source's motion raises the frequency heard.
That is the frequency for a receding source.

questions.prompt: A sound has an intensity of 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ W/m². Using I₀ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹² W/m², what is its level, in decibels, to the nearest decibel?
hints: log₁₀ 2 is about 0.30, so the log is 7.30.
questions.onCorrect: The factor of 2 in 2.0 × 10⁷ contributes about 3 dB on top of the 70 dB for 10⁷.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the 2.0. The ratio is 2.0 × 10⁷, not 10⁷.
That is the logarithm. Multiply it by 10 to get decibels.

questions.prompt: Four identical sources each give a level of 65 dB at your position. What is the level when all four sound together, in decibels, to the nearest decibel?
hints: Intensities add, so the intensity is four times that of one source.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Four times the intensity adds 10 log₁₀ 4 = 6.0 dB: 65 + 6 = 71 dB.

questions.onCorrect: Four times the intensity is two doublings, which is two steps of 3 dB, so +6 dB.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the levels. Levels follow the logarithm of the total intensity.
That adds only 3 dB, for a doubling. Four sources give four times the intensity.

questions.prompt: A train horn sounds at 400 Hz while the train approaches a still listener at 20 m/s. The speed of sound is 343 m/s. What frequency does the listener hear, to the nearest hertz?
hints: The source is moving towards a still listener.
questions.onCorrect: The approaching source shortens the wavelength, so the horn is heard at about 425 Hz.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the frequency the horn emits. The approach raises the frequency heard.
That is the frequency for a receding source.

questions.prompt: Diamond has a refractive index of 2.42, and the speed of light in a vacuum is 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. What is the speed of light in diamond, in units of 10⁸ m/s, to two decimal places?
hints: The index n is the factor by which light slows.
questions.onCorrect: The speed in diamond is 1.24 × 10⁸ m/s, well under half the speed in a vacuum. A larger refractive index always means a slower speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by n. Light is slower in diamond, so divide.
That is the speed in a vacuum. The diamond slows it.

questions.prompt: A ray of light in air meets a flat sheet of glass at an angle to the normal, the line at right angles to the surface, rather than along it. On entering the glass, the ray bends
hints: Picture a wavefront arriving at an angle. The end that reaches the glass first slows first, while the other end is still moving fast. Which way does the front pivot?
questions.onCorrect: Entering the slower medium, the ray bends toward the normal, which is the line at right angles to the surface.

misconceptions.feedback: Light slows in the glass, which turns the ray towards the normal, not away from it.
A ray does not run along the surface except at one special angle, going out of glass.
A ray meeting the surface at an angle changes direction; only a ray along the normal enters undeviated.

choices.label: Along the surface
Not at all
Away from the normal
Toward the normal

questions.prompt: A ray in air meets glass of index 1.50 at 45°, where sin 45° = 0.707. What is sin θ₂, to three decimal places?
hints: The answer is a little less than a half.
questions.onCorrect: The sine of the refracted angle is 0.471. Its arcsine is then the angle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 1.50 × 0.707, the sum for light going from glass to air, and a sine above 1 has no angle. Here the 1.50 is on the denominator.
That divides 1.50 by 0.707. The glass index is the divisor.

questions.prompt: What is arcsin(0.483), in degrees to one decimal place?
hints: Use the inverse sine key on a calculator, in degree mode.
sin 30° is 0.500, so the angle is a little under 30°.
Check the calculator is in degree mode, not radians.
questions.onCorrect: The ray bends from 40° to 28.9°, towards the normal, because water has a higher index than air.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sine of the angle. Take the inverse sine to find the angle.
That is the angle in the air. The ray bends in the water.

questions.prompt: Light travels upwards inside water, of index 1.33, towards the surface, where it meets air of index 1.00. What is the critical angle for water to air, in degrees to one decimal place?
hints: The light goes from n₁ = 1.33 to n₂ = 1.00.
questions.onCorrect: Water has a smaller refractive index than glass, so its critical angle of 48.8° is larger than glass's 41.8°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the critical angle for glass. Use n = 1.33 for water.
That is the sine of the angle. Take the inverse sine.

questions.prompt: A ray inside a glass block of index 1.50 meets the flat top surface, which borders air, at 25° to the normal. At what angle to the normal does the ray emerge into the air, in degrees to one decimal place?
questions.onCorrect: The ray bends away from the normal, from 25° to 39.3°. A 25° ray is well below the critical angle of 41.8°, so it escapes.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 1.50, as for light entering glass. Here the ray is leaving it.
The ray changes direction at the surface. Use Snell's law.

questions.prompt: A ray in air meets glass of index 1.50 at 50° to the normal. What is the angle of the ray in the glass, in degrees to one decimal place?
hints: Use n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with n₁ = 1.00.
Divide by 1.50 and take the arcsine.
questions.onCorrect: The ray bends from 50° to 30.7°, towards the normal.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sine of the angle. Take the arcsine.
That is the angle in the air. The ray bends in the glass.

questions.prompt: A glass has a refractive index of 1.60. What is the critical angle for light going from this glass to air, in degrees to one decimal place?
questions.onCorrect: A higher refractive index gives a smaller critical angle, 38.7° here compared with 41.8° for index 1.50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sine of the angle. Take the inverse sine.
That has the indices the wrong way round, 1.60 / 1.00 cannot be a sine.

questions.prompt: A ray in water (n = 1.33) meets glass (n = 1.50) at 35° to the normal. What is its angle in the glass, in degrees to one decimal place?
hints: Medium 1 is water and medium 2 is glass.
Put n₁ sin θ₁ on top, and n₂ underneath.
questions.onCorrect: The glass has the higher index, so the ray bends towards the normal again, from 35° to 30.6°.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the angle in the water. The indices differ, so the ray bends.
That swaps the indices. The ray goes into the higher index, so the angle gets smaller.

questions.prompt: A converging lens has a focal length of 10 cm. An object 30 cm from it gives an image 15 cm behind it, and an object 15 cm from it gives an image 30 cm behind it. Where does the image form when the object is 20 cm from the lens, twice the focal length?
hints: Look for a pattern in the two cases shown in the figure.
The distances 30 and 15 swap places in the two cases.
questions.onCorrect: At twice the focal length the image is the same distance from the lens as the object, and the same size.

misconceptions.feedback: An object at 30 cm gives an image at 15 cm, and bringing the object nearer pushes the image farther away. Ask which way the image moves for an object at 20 cm.
An object at 15 cm gives an image at 30 cm, and moving the object farther away brings the image nearer. Ask which way the image moves for an object at 20 cm.
An object outside the focal length always gives a real image on the far side of the lens, so an image does form.

choices.label: Closer than 15 cm behind the lens
Farther than 30 cm behind the lens
Nowhere, because no image forms at that distance
About 20 cm behind the lens

questions.prompt: What is d_i, in centimetres, if 1/d_i = 1/12 cm⁻¹?
hints: The reciprocal of a fraction turns it upside down.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: d_i is the reciprocal of 1/12, which is 12 cm.

questions.onCorrect: The image forms 12 cm beyond the lens, a little beyond the focal point because the object is far away. Remember that the 1/d_i you work out is not yet a distance until it is inverted.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 1/12 as a decimal. Take the reciprocal to find the distance.
That is the object distance. The image is nearer to the lens.

questions.prompt: A lens of focal length 15 cm forms an image of an object 45 cm away. What is the image distance, in centimetres?
questions.onCorrect: The image is 22.5 cm from the lens, on the far side.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2/45 as a decimal. Invert it.
That is the object distance, not the image distance.

questions.prompt: A lens forms an image 22.5 cm from the lens of an object 45 cm away. What is the magnification, as a signed number?
hints: Keep the minus sign in the formula.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: m = −d_i/d_o = −22.5/45 = −0.5, which is inverted and half size.

questions.onCorrect: A magnification of −0.5 means the image is upside down and half the height of the object.

misconceptions.feedback: The formula has a minus sign: this is a real image, so it is inverted.
That inverts the ratio. Use d_i / d_o with d_i on top.

questions.prompt: An object stands 8 cm from a converging lens whose focal length is 12 cm. What kind of image does the lens form?
hints: Is the object nearer than f, or farther?
Are the rays converging after the lens, or still diverging?
questions.onCorrect: Inside the focal length the rays still diverge after the lens, so the image is virtual, upright and larger.

misconceptions.feedback: A real image needs rays that cross, which happens only when the object is beyond the focal length.
The image is larger, but a real image would be inverted and needs rays that cross, which they do not inside f.
An image does form: the rays appear to come from a point behind the object.

choices.label: Real, inverted and smaller
Real, inverted and larger
No image forms
Virtual, upright and larger

questions.prompt: A converging lens of focal length 10 cm is held 6 cm from a small object, as a magnifying glass is. What is the image distance d_i, in centimetres? Use a negative number for a virtual image.
hints: Take the reciprocal and keep the sign.
questions.onCorrect: The image is 15 cm from the lens on the object's side. It is two and a half times as far away as the object, which makes it two and a half times as large.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign matters. A positive d_i would be a real image beyond the lens.
That is the object distance. The image is farther than the object.
That adds 1/10 and 1/6. Rearranged for the image, the equation subtracts: 1/d_i = 1/f − 1/d_o.

questions.prompt: A camera lens has a focal length of 50 mm and is focused on a person standing 2.0 m, which is 2000 mm, from the lens. How far behind the lens must the sensor be, in millimetres?
hints: Use the thin-lens equation with every length in millimetres.
questions.onCorrect: A distant object puts the image almost at the focal point, 50 mm. At 2.0 m the sensor sits 1.3 mm farther back.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the focal length, the image distance for an object at infinity. The person is at 2.0 m.
That subtracts rather than adds the small difference. The image is further from the lens than f.

questions.prompt: A lens has a focal length of 12 cm. An object stands 20 cm from the lens. How far from the lens is the image, in centimetres?
questions.onCorrect: The image is 30 cm beyond the lens, farther than the object because the object is between f and 2f.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the reciprocals, 1/12 + 1/20. The image distance comes from their difference.
That subtracts the distances, 20 − 12. The equation works with reciprocals.

questions.prompt: A lens of focal length 8.0 cm is held 6.0 cm from an object. What is the image distance, in centimetres? Use a negative number for a virtual image.
hints: The object is inside the focal length.
questions.onCorrect: The image is virtual, 24 cm from the lens on the object's side, and the magnification is +4.

misconceptions.feedback: The sign matters: a positive value would mean a real image, but the object is inside f.
That subtracts the distances. Use the reciprocals.

questions.prompt: A lens of focal length 25 cm forms an image of an object 100 cm away. What is the magnification, as a signed number to two decimal places?
questions.onCorrect: The image is inverted and one third the height of the object.

misconceptions.feedback: The minus sign matters: a real image is inverted.
That inverts the ratio. Use d_i / d_o.

questions.prompt: A balloon rubbed on wool carries a negative charge, and it is held close to some small pieces of neutral paper, which carry no net charge. What does the balloon do to the pieces of paper?
hints: The paper contains charges of both signs.
Which part of the paper is nearer to the balloon, and how strongly is it pulled?
questions.onCorrect: A charged object polarises a neutral one, so the near side takes the opposite sign and the pull on it wins.

misconceptions.feedback: The balloon's charge shifts the charge inside each piece, so the nearer side is the opposite sign and is pulled more strongly. The result is a net attraction.
The paper has no net charge, but its charges are still able to move a little, and the balloon pulls on the nearer ones harder.

choices.label: It attracts them
It has no effect on them
It repels them

questions.prompt: A rubbed rod ends up with a charge of −1.0 µC, where 1 µC = 10⁻⁶ C, because electrons have moved onto it, and each electron carries 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. How many electrons moved onto the rod, in units of 10¹²?
hints: Total charge = number of electrons × the charge of one electron.
The result is a few times 10¹².
questions.onCorrect: A charge of one microcoulomb is carried by about 6.24 × 10¹² electrons.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the charge of one electron in different units. Divide the total charge by it to count them.
That multiplies instead of dividing. N = Q / e.

questions.prompt: What is (0.30 m)², in square metres?
questions.onCorrect: The separation is squared, so 0.30 m gives 0.090 m² on the bottom of the fraction.

misconceptions.feedback: That doubles 0.30. The separation is squared.
That is 0.30 × 3. Multiply 0.30 by itself.

questions.prompt: Two charges repel each other with some force. If their separation is made three times as large, with the charges unchanged, how does the force change?
hints: The force depends on r², not on r.
What happens to r² when r triples?

acceptedIdeas: It becomes a ninth as large
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It becomes a ninth as large

questions.onCorrect: Tripling the distance divides the force by 9, which is 0.111 of its original size.

misconceptions.feedback: The force falls faster than the distance grows, since doubling the distance already gives a quarter of the force, and tripling it leaves a ninth.
Moving charges farther apart weakens the force between them, and tripling the distance leaves a ninth of the original force.
The force depends on the separation as well as on the charges, and tripling the separation leaves a ninth of the force.

choices.label: It becomes a ninth as large
It becomes three times as large
It becomes a third as large
It stays the same, because the charges are unchanged

questions.prompt: What is (3.0 × 10⁻⁶)(2.0 × 10⁻⁶), in units of 10⁻¹² C²?
hints: Multiply 3.0 by 2.0, then the powers of ten.
questions.onCorrect: The charge product is 6.0 × 10⁻¹² C². Only the sizes of the charges matter for the magnitude of the force.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the charges. The force depends on their product.
That subtracts. Multiply the two charges.

questions.prompt: A 3.0 µC charge and a −2.0 µC charge are 0.15 m apart. What is the size of the force between them, in newtons to two decimal places?
hints: Substitute k, the product of the charges and r².
questions.onCorrect: The force is 2.40 N, attractive because the charges have opposite signs.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by r rather than r². The separation is squared.
That is the numerator alone. Divide by r² = 0.0225.

questions.prompt: Two 1.0 µC charges 0.10 m apart repel with a force of 0.899 N. If they are moved to 0.30 m apart, what is the force, in newtons to three decimal places?
hints: Tripling the distance changes the force by a factor of 1/3².
Divide the force at 0.10 m by 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: F = 0.899 N / 3² = 0.0999 N, or 0.100 N to three decimal places.

questions.onCorrect: At three times the separation the force is one ninth of what it was.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by three. The force follows an inverse square, so tripling the distance divides it by nine.
That multiplies by nine. A greater separation weakens the force.
That is the force at 0.20 m, twice the distance. At 0.30 m the factor is 1/3².

questions.prompt: In a hydrogen atom the electron is about 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m from the proton, and the two carry charges of equal size, 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, with opposite signs. What is the size of the electric force between them, in newtons? Give your answer in standard form, such as 3.5e-6.
hints: Both charges have the size e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
Square e for the product, and 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ for r².
questions.onCorrect: A force of 8.2 × 10⁻⁸ N gives the electron an acceleration of about 10²³ m/s², which keeps it in orbit around the proton.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the top of the fraction. Divide by r².
That divides by r rather than r². The separation is squared.

questions.prompt: Two charges of 4.0 µC and 5.0 µC are 0.50 m apart. What is the size of the force between them, in newtons to two decimal places?
hints: Multiply by k and divide by 0.25.
questions.onCorrect: The force is 0.72 N. The force depends on the product of the two charges, so the two different sizes combine into one number.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by r rather than r².
That leaves the charges in microcoulombs. Convert to coulombs.
